entry.title: SAP Fiori Tools 2607 Update: Skills, Fullstack AI Development, and Performance
entry.content:
The 2607 release of SAP Fiori tools focuses on AI-driven development, but there is also good news for the human tooling: faster startup, more Page Editor capabilities, and a few quality-of-life fixes. Here is what is new.

AI-Driven Development with the MCP Server for SAP Fiori

MCP support in SAP Business Application Studio

SAP Business Application Studio now includes an AI Chat capability that you can use for MCP-supported AI-driven SAP Fiori development directly from the browser. No installation is needed: the MCP server for SAP Fiori comes pre-installed in SAP Fiori and Fullstack Dev spaces, alongside the UI5 and CAP MCP servers.

Installing the MCP server locally

For local development, the MCP server for SAP Fiori is now available through the MCP registry on GitHub. You can also install it as a Claude plugin, together with our new skills (more on that below).

By the way, if you have the SAP Fiori tools extension pack installed in VS Code, you automatically have a version of the MCP server for SAP Fiori available that can be consumed by the GitHub Copilot extension.

Skills: the next layer on top of MCP

MCP servers provide the tools an AI agent can call, but tools alone do not tell the agent how to approach a complex, multi-step development job. That is the job of a skill. A skill bundles domain knowledge, step-by-step guidance, and best practices into a reusable prompt-based workflow that directs the AI through a specific task. Instead of leaving the model to figure out the right sequence of tool calls on its own, a skill encodes that knowledge explicitly, leading to more reliable and consistent results.

With this release, the SAP Fiori tools team publishes the first set of skills that complement the MCP server for SAP Fiori:

SkillWhat it does
sap-fiori-app-developmentGuides the creation and modification of SAP Fiori elements applications in CAP and standalone projects
sap-fiori-analytical-chartAdds an analytical chart and table hybrid to a List Report, supporting CAP and ABAP RAP (OData V4)
sap-fiori-add-visual-filterAdds chart-based visual filters to the filter bar or value help in SAP Fiori elements applications
sap-fiori-create-cliRuns and automates the @​sap-ux/create CLI for generating, converting, and managing Fiori projects
sap-fiori-eslint-pluginConfigures, migrates, or runs ESLint with the @​sap-ux/eslint-plugin-fiori-tools in SAP Fiori projects

The easiest way to get the skills is through the Claude plugin, where they are included alongside the MCP server for SAP Fiori. Alternatively, you can install individual skills via skills.sh, an open ecosystem for reusable agent skills that supports Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and others.

We will continuously expand and improve this set of skills, and we are very much looking forward to your feedback.

Fullstack development in VS Code

The MCP server for SAP Fiori pairs with the new ABAP MCP server, which is part of the ABAP development tools for Visual Studio Code. Together, the two bridge the gap between backend ABAP services and the SAP Fiori frontend, enabling a true fullstack AI-driven development experience from within VS Code. For a concrete walkthrough of how this can look in practice, I recommend watching my ABAPConf presentation.

A new top-level tool structure

Based on feedback we have collected from usage, we restructured the top-level tools of the MCP server for SAP Fiori. More capabilities are now surfaced directly at the top level, in particular the app generators and metadata retrieval, which are needed to properly connect backend services to the frontend layer. This restructuring is available as of version 1.8.1 of the MCP server for SAP Fiori.

The top-level tools now are:

ToolWhat it does
search_docsSearches SAP Fiori elements, annotations, UI5, OPA5, and SAP Fiori tools documentation
list_fiori_appsScans a directory to find existing SAP Fiori applications
list_sap_systemsLists SAP systems stored in the user's environment
download_odata_service_metadataDownloads the EDMX metadata of an OData service from an SAP system
generate_fiori_app_odataGenerates a new SAP Fiori application for OData (non-CAP) projects, for example RAP-based services
generate_fiori_app_capGenerates a new SAP Fiori application inside an existing CAP project
list_functionality (Step 1 of 3)Lists supported modification operations for an existing SAP Fiori application
get_functionality_details (Step 2 of 3)Returns the required parameters for a chosen modification
execute_functionality (Step 3 of 3)Executes the modification with the provided parameters

This structure also sets the stage for what comes next. We are working on adaptation project support for the MCP server for SAP Fiori, which will add tools for creating and modifying adaptation projects directly through AI agents. They will join the top-level structure shown above.

Renovations and Performance Improvements

Moving from CommonJS to ECMAScript Modules

ECMAScript Modules (ESM) are the official JavaScript module standard, supported natively in modern browsers and Node.js. With this release, the SAP Fiori tools suite and its Node.js modules migrate from CommonJS to ESM. For us, this means better ecosystem compatibility, tree-shaking for smaller bundles (unused code eliminated at build time), and more efficient asynchronous module loading.

ESLint 10 upgrade

The 2603 release delivered ESLint 9 support for the tools and generator. With 2607 we take the next step and upgrade to ESLint 10, keeping the toolchain current and continuing the move toward the modern flat config format.

80% faster extension startup

As the SAP Fiori tools extensions have grown over time, startup time had crept up correspondingly. Through targeted refactoring and more efficient bundling, loading only what is necessary at startup, we reduced the startup time of the SAP Fiori tools extensions by around 80%.

Other Improvements

A few smaller additions that are worth calling out:

  • Fiori Generator error details: Clicking on an error in the generator now opens the full error details in the console, making it much easier to diagnose what went wrong.
  • Page Editor building blocks: The Page Editor now supports Page, Form, and Field building blocks in custom pages and custom sections, rounding out the building block coverage for custom development.
  • SAP Fiori elements enhancements via Page Editor: The Page Editor now lets you configure a notes reuse component, inline edit, mass edit, and creation dialogs (and more) for SAP Fiori elements applications, all through the graphical configuration interface without touching annotations manually.
  • Reuse existing LineItem annotations for tables: When adding a table, you can now select an existing LineItem annotation from the service instead of always having to create a new one. This avoids duplicate annotations and makes it easier to build UIs on top of well-annotated services.
  • Unique control IDs in XML generation: The Page Editor now correctly generates unique control IDs when producing XML for custom elements.
  • Download UI5 ABAP repository content from the public cloud: You can now download source artifacts directly from a deployed SAPUI5 ABAP repository, so you can continue local development even when the source files are not available. This closes a gap for public cloud customers, who previously had no way to import from the ABAP backend. See the SAP Help Portal documentation for more information.

Staying Up to Date

If you want to track changes in SAP Fiori tools between release blog posts, the What's New section in the SAP Help Portal is the best place to look. It is updated continuously with newly delivered capabilities and fixes.

For documentation and sample code covering all building blocks available when creating SAP Fiori elements applications, visit the SAP Fiori development portal.

Questions and feedback? Leave a comment below or reach out through the community.

entry.title: Getting Started with GitHub in SAP Business Application Studio for SAP UI5 Development
entry.content:
Overview:

SAP Business Application Studio (BAS) trial accounts expire every 90 days, making it essential to safeguard SAP UI5 projects using a reliable version control system. GitHub not only helps prevent project loss but also introduces the collaboration practices widely used in professional software development.

This blog covers:

  • Connecting SAP Business Application Studio (BAS) with GitHub
  • Step-by-step process to push and manage SAP UI5 projects using GitHub.

The intent is to provide a simple and practical guide for SAP UI5 learners and developers to protect their projects, understand Git and GitHub fundamentals, and adopt industry-standard version control practices.

Introduction:

When I started learning SAP UI5, I was using a trial account on SAP Business Application Studio (BAS). 

Everything was going great — until I hit my first big obstacle. 

  • Every 90 days, the trial account expires. And when it does, everything is gone. All my projects. All my code. Vanished. 

My only option back then was to manually download each project as a zip file to my desktop before the account reset. Then when the new trial started, I had to upload everything back again. 

It was painful. It was repetitive. And one time, I forgot — and lost a project I had worked on for weeks. 

That's when I discovered GitHub — and it completely changed how I work.

I started learning how to:

  • Upload my SAP UI5 projects from SAP Business Application Studio (BAS) to GitHub.
  • Access them anytime, from anywhere, even after my BAS trial account resets.
  • Share my projects easily with teammates and collaborate more effectively.
  • No more downloading ZIP files. No more worrying about the 90-day deadline. My code was safely stored in the cloud, always accessible, and backed by version control.

What Is GitHub and Why Do We Need It?

The easiest way to think about GitHub is this: it's like Google Docs for source code. Instead of collaborating on documents, developers collaborate on code while Git keeps track of every change.

GitHub is a cloud-based platform built on top of Git, a distributed version control system. It enables developers to store their source code in the cloud, track changes over time, and collaborate with others while maintaining a complete history of every modification.

In addition to version control, GitHub provides features such as repositories, branches, pull requests, and code reviews, making it easier for individuals and teams to manage software projects efficiently.

Although GitHub is widely used for open-source development, it is equally important in enterprise environments. Development teams use it to collaborate on projects, review code, manage changes, and maintain high-quality software throughout the development lifecycle.

GitHub is not just a tool for beginners. It is an industry-standard platform used by organizations of all sizes to support real-world software development and team collaboration.

In real-world software projects, developers rarely work alone. Front-end developers, backend developers, testers, and other team members often work on the same application simultaneously. Without a version control platform like GitHub, collaboration can quickly become difficult, with developers accidentally overwriting each other's changes and having no clear way to track who changed what or revert to previous versions.

GitHub solves this challenge through features such as branching. Think of the main project as a tree trunk, where each developer creates their own branch to work independently on a feature, enhancement, or bug fix. Once the work is complete, the changes are reviewed through a Pull Request (PR) and then merged back into the main branch.

This approach enables multiple developers to work in parallel without interfering with one another, maintains a complete history of code changes, and ensures that every update is reviewed before becoming part of the main project. As a result, GitHub has become an industry-standard platform for version control and team collaboration in professional software development.

A Typical Team Workflow
A typical GitHub workflow in a development team looks like this:

 
main branch          → Stable, production-ready code

├── developer-1      → Working on the Login feature
├── developer-2      → Working on the Dashboard feature
└── developer-3      → Fixing a bug in the Search feature

Each developer works on their own branch without affecting the work of others. Once a feature or bug fix is complete, the developer creates a Pull Request (PR) to request that their changes be reviewed before they are merged into the main branch.

A senior developer or technical lead reviews the code, provides feedback if any changes are required, and approves the Pull Request once the code meets the project's quality standards. After approval, the changes are merged into the main branch.

This workflow helps ensure:

  • Developers can work independently without interfering with one another.
  • Every code change is reviewed before being merged.

A complete history of changes is maintained, making it easy to track who changed what and when.

The main branch remains stable and ready for deployment.

 Now, let's walk through the step-by-step process of connecting SAP Business Application Studio (BAS) to GitHub and uploading your SAP UI5 project.

Step- 1: Create a GitHub Account

  • Sign up for a GitHub account if you don't already have one.

Step 2: Initialize the Git Repository

  • Open your SAP UI5 project in SAP Business Application Studio (BAS).
  • Open the Terminal by navigating to Terminal → New Terminal.

    Run the following command to initialize a Git repository with main as the default branch:
git init -b main​

This command initializes a new Git repository in your project directory and creates the default branch named main. Git will now start tracking changes made to your project.

Step 3: Stage All Project Files

  • After initializing the Git repository, stage all the project files by running the following command in the terminal:
git add .​
  • The git add . command stages all the files and folders in the current project directory. Staging tells Git which changes should be included in the next commit.
  • Once the files are staged, Git is ready to create a snapshot of your project using a commit.
  • Note: The . (dot) represents the current directory, so git add . stages all files within your project.

Step 4: Commit the Changes

  • Once all the project files have been staged, create your first commit by running the following command:
git commit -m "Vendor Details"​
  • Creates a commit with the message "Vendor Details", which serves as a snapshot of your project at its current state.
  • Verify the Commit
  • To confirm that the commit was created successfully, run the following command:
  • git log
  • Displays the commit history of the repository, including the commit ID, author, date, and commit message.
  • If the commit was successful, you should see an output similar to:
commit 3f2c9b8e6d4f1a2b...
Author: <Your Name> <your-email@example.com>
Date:   Sat Jun 6 10:30:15 2026

    Vendor Details​
  • This confirms that your project has been committed successfully and Git is now tracking this version of your code.

Step 5: Configure Git (First-Time Setup)

  • If you're using Git for the first time, configure your username and email address using the following commands:
git config --global user.name "<github_username>"
git config --global user.email "<github_email>"
  • Configures your Git username and email address. These details are associated with every commit you create.

Step 6: Create a GitHub Repository

  • Sign in to your GitHub account.
  • Click New Repository.
  • Enter a repository name (for example, Vendor_Details_App).
  • Click Create repository.

Step 7: Connect the Local Repository to GitHub

  • After creating the repository, copy its HTTPS URL and run the following command in the BAS terminal:
git remote add origin https://github.com/sap-honey/Vendor_Details_App.git
  • Connects your local Git repository to the remote GitHub repository.

Step 8: Push the Project to GitHub

  • Push your local commits to the remote GitHub repository using the following command:
git push -u origin main​
  • Uploads your local main branch to the remote GitHub repository. The -u option sets the upstream branch, so future pushes can be performed simply by running:
git push​

  • When you run the git push command for the first time, GitHub prompts you to authenticate your account.

  • Click Copy and Open GitHub.

  • This copies the verification code and opens the GitHub device activation page in your browser.
  • GitHub automatically opens the device activation page. If prompted, sign in to your GitHub account.
  • Paste the verification code and click Continue, then click Authorize to grant SAP Business Application Studio permission to access your GitHub repository.
  • After the authorization is complete, return to SAP Business Application Studio. The git push command will finish automatically.
  • Open your GitHub account and navigate to the repository you created.
  • Refresh the repository page. You should now see all your SAP UI5 project files successfully uploaded.

    This confirms that your local SAP UI5 project has been successfully pushed to GitHub. From now on, you only need to commit your changes and run:

git push​

GitHub is an essential tool for every SAP UI5 developer. By connecting SAP Business Application Studio with GitHub, you can securely store your projects, track changes, and continue your work even after a BAS trial reset.

I hope this blog helps you get started with GitHub and makes managing your SAP UI5 projects easier and more efficient. Happy coding!

entry.title: Trigger SAP Build Process Automation Workflow from Fiori Application
entry.content:
In this blog, we will learn how to trigger an SAP Build Process Automation (BPA) workflow directly from a SAPUI5/Fiori application.

This approach is useful when users need to start approval processes, requests, or business workflows directly from the application UI.

Prerequisites

Before starting, make sure the following things are done:

  1. Cloud Identity Services must be subscribed.
  2. SAP Build Process Automation must be subscribed.
  3. SAP Build Work Zone must be subscribed.
  4. Workflow must be deployed successfully.
  5. User must have the role: “ProcessAutomationParticipant”

Note: Workflow triggering from the UI will work after deployment because BPA runtime is accessed through destinations configured in SAP BTP.

You can find the complete implementation here: https://github.com/MaheshSirsat/trigger-bpa-workflow-from-fiori/tree/main 

Step 1 – Fetch SAP Build Process Automation Credentials

We need runtime credentials from the SAP Build Process Automation instance. These credentials will be used while creating the destination.

Navigation

  1. Open SAP BTP Cockpit.
  2. Go to Instances and Subscriptions.
  3. Locate your SAP Build Process Automation instance.

 

  1. Open the instance.
  2. Click View Credentials.

 

 

The credentials contain:

  • API endpoint URL
  • OAuth client ID
  • Client secret
  • Token URL

These details allow our Fiori application to communicate securely with the BPA runtime.

Step 2 – Create Destination

We create a destination that acts as a secure bridge between the Fiori application and the SAP Build Process Automation APIs.

Navigation

  1. Open Destinations
  2. Click Create Destination

 

 

 

Configuration

Name : sap_build_process_automation

URL : endpoints.api

Authentication : OAuth2JWTBearer

Client ID : uaa.clientid

Client Secret : uaa.clientsecret

Token Service URL : uaa.url/oauth/token

Additional Properties

 

endpoints : <copy complete endpoints object>

html5-apps-repo : <copy complete html5-apps-repo object>

saasregistryenabled : true

sap.cloud.service : com.sap.spa.processautomation

sap.cloud.service.alias : spa

The destination stores all connectivity information required to call BPA APIs. Instead of hardcoding credentials inside the application, SAP BTP securely manages them through the destination.

Step 3 – Create Fiori Application

Create a SAPUI5/Fiori application that will contain a button to start the workflow.

You can create:

  • Freestyle Application
  • List Report Application

After creation, run the application locally and ensure it opens successfully.

 

Step 4 – Configure xs-app.json

Add the following route inside xs-app.json:

{

  "source": "^/workflow/(.*)$",

  "target": "/public/workflow/rest/$1",

  "destination": "sap_build_process_automation",

  "authenticationType": "xsuaa",

  "csrfProtection": false

}

 

Whenever the application calls:

/workflow/*

the App Router automatically forwards the request to the destination configured earlier.

Step 5 – Create Workflow Trigger Button

Add a button in the UI:

<mvc:View
    controllerName="project2.controller.View1"
    xmlns:mvc="sap.ui.core.mvc"
    xmlns="sap.m">
    <Page title="Workflow Demo">
        <Button  text="Start WF"  press="onstartWF"/>
    </Page>
</mvc:View>

 

The button allows users to start the workflow directly from the UI.

Step 6 – Implement Workflow Trigger Logic

Create the following function inside the controller:

   onstartWF: async function () {
            var data = {
                definitionId: "myworkflow", // workflow-defination-id
                context: { "name": "mahesh" } // your context
            };
            await $.ajax({
                url: this._getWorkflowRuntimeBaseURL() + "/workflow-instances",
                method: "POST",
                async: false,
                contentType: "application/json",

                data: JSON.stringify(data),
                success: function (result, xhr, data) {
                    sap.m.MessageToast.show('Workflow started successfully...')
                },
                error: function (request, status, error) {
                    console.error('Error in Trigger workflow')
                }
            });
        },

 

This code sends a POST request to the BPA runtime API and creates a new workflow instance.

Understanding the Payload

{
    definitionId: "myworkflow",
    context: {        "name": "mahesh"    }
}

definitionId

definitionId: "myworkflow"

This is the workflow definition ID of the deployed workflow.

 

BPA uses this value to identify which workflow should be started.

context

context: {

    "name": "mahesh"

}

This data becomes the workflow context and can be accessed inside forms, approvals, conditions, and automation steps.

Step 7 – Generate Runtime URL

Create the helper method:

_getWorkflowRuntimeBaseURL: function () {
    var appId =this.getOwnerComponent().getManifestEntry("/sap.app/id");
    var appPath =appId.replaceAll(".", "/");
    var appModulePath = jQuery.sap.getModulePath(appPath);
    return appModulePath + "/workflow/v1";
}

 

Instead of hardcoding BPA URLs, the application uses the App Router route configured in xs-app.json.

 

Step 8 – Build and Deploy Application

Build the application:

Deploy it to SAP BTP.

 

The workflow runtime destination and App Router configuration are available only after deployment.

Step 9 – Create Catalog, Group, and Role in Work Zone

After deployment:

  1. Create Catalog
  2. Create Group
  3. Create Role
  4. Assign application tile
  5. Assign role to user

Step 10 – Test from Launchpad

  1. Open SAP Build Work Zone.
  2. Launch the application.
  3. Click Start WF.

Expected result:

Workflow started successfully...

 

You can verify the workflow instance in SAP Build Process Automation Monitoring.

Final Result

We have successfully triggered an SAP Build Process Automation workflow directly from a Fiori application.

✔ BPA credentials are retrieved from the BPA instance.

✔ Destination securely manages authentication and connectivity.

✔ xs-app.json routes requests through App Router.

✔ UI button initiates workflow execution.

✔ Workflow context can be passed dynamically from the application.

✔ Users can start workflows directly from SAP Build Work Zone.

entry.title: Creating a Custom Action to Export Selected Records to Excel Using Fiori Elements and CAP
entry.content:
Introduction

While working on a Fiori Elements application, I came across a requirement that initially seemed straightforward but wasn't available as a standard feature. The application already had the built-in Export to Excel option, but it always exported every row displayed in the table. The business users wanted something slightly different—they wanted to select only a few records and export just those.

My first thought was to implement a backend action that generated an Excel file and returned it to the UI. After exploring the available options, I realized that wasn't necessary. SAPUI5 already provides a Spreadsheet API that can generate Excel files directly in the browser, making the implementation much simpler while avoiding additional backend development.

In this blog, I'll walk through the approach I used to add a custom Export Selected button to a Fiori Elements List Report. By the end, you'll have a working example that exports only the selected rows and integrates naturally with the standard Fiori toolbar.

Step 1: Initialize the CAP Project

First, create a new directory for your project and initialize a standard SAP CAP application. Open your terminal and run:

mkdir employee
cd employee
cds init

Step 2: Define the Database Schema

Next, we will define the data model for our employees.

Create a file named schema.cds inside the db folder and add the following code:

// db/schema.cds
namespace company.hr;
 
entity Employees {
    key ID     : UUID;
    name       : String;
    department : String;
    role       : String;
    email      : String;
}

Step 3: Create the Service and UI Annotations

Now, expose the database entity as an OData service and add the basic Fiori UI annotations to define what columns will appear in our Fiori List Report table.

Create a file named cat-services.cds (typically in the srv folder) and add this code:

// srv/cat-services.cds
using { company.hr as db } from '../db/schema';
 
service EmployeeService {
    entity Employees as projection on db.Employees;
}
 
annotate EmployeeService.Employees with @(
    UI.LineItem : [
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : 'Employee Name', Value : name },
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : 'Department', Value : department },
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : 'Role', Value : role },
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : 'Email', Value : email }
    ]
);

Step 4: Add Mock Data

To test our application, we need some dummy data. SAP CAP automatically loads CSV files that match the namespace and entity.

Create a folder named data inside your db folder, then create a file named company.hr-Employees.csv and paste the following:

ID;name;department;role;email
1;Alice Walker;Engineering;Backend Developer;alice@company.com
2;Bob Smith;Sales;Account Executive;bob@company.com
3;Charlie Davis;Engineering;Frontend Developer;charlie@company.com
4;Diana Prince;HR;HR Manager;diana@company.com

Step 5: Configure the Custom Action in the Page Map

Once your Fiori Elements application has been generated, the next step is to add a custom action to the table toolbar.

Follow these steps:

  1. Right-click on the webapp folder in your project.
  2. Select Show Page Map.
  3. In the Page Map, select the List Report page.
  4. Click the Edit (pencil) icon to modify the page.
  5. Under the Table / Table Toolbar section, click the + button next to Actions.
  6. Select Add Custom Action.

Configure the custom action with the following properties:

  • Label: Export Selected
  • Requires Selection: Enabled
  • Press Event: exportSelected

Step 6: Implement the Custom UI5 Export Logic

Now, we will write the logic that extracts the selected rows and converts them to an Excel file using the Fiori V4 API.

Open the newly generated controller extension file (ListReportExt.js) and replace its contents with the following:

sap.ui.define([
    "sap/ui/export/Spreadsheet",
    "sap/m/MessageToast"
], function (Spreadsheet, MessageToast) {
    "use strict";
 
    return {
        exportSelected: function (oEvent) {
            
            // 1. Access the Fiori V4 API
            var oExtensionAPI = this.editFlow ? this : this.getExtensionAPI();
            
            // 2. Get only the rows selected by the user
            var aSelection = oExtensionAPI.getSelectedContexts();
 
            if (!aSelection || aSelection.length === 0) {
                MessageToast.show("Please select at least one employee to export.");
                return;
            }
 
            // 3. Extract the raw JSON data from those selected rows
            var aData = aSelection.map(function (oContext) {
                return oContext.getObject();
            });
 
            // 4. Map the Excel columns to your CDS database fields
            var aColumns = [
                { label: 'Employee Name', property: 'name' },
                { label: 'Department', property: 'department' },
                { label: 'Role', property: 'role' },
                { label: 'Email', property: 'email' }
            ];
 
            // 5. Configure the Excel Workbook properties
            var oSettings = {
                workbook: { 
                    columns: aColumns,
                    context: {
                        sheetName: 'Selected Employees'
                    }
                },
                dataSource: aData,
                fileName: "Custom_Employee_Export.xlsx",
                worker: false 
            };
 
            // 6. Build and Download the Excel file
            var oSheet = new Spreadsheet(oSettings);
            
            oSheet.build().then(function() {
                MessageToast.show("Excel export successful!");
            }).catch(function(sMessage) {
                MessageToast.show("Export failed: " + sMessage);
            }).finally(function () {
                oSheet.destroy(); // Destroy object to prevent memory leaks in the browser
            });
        }
    };
});

Step 7: Run and Test the Application

With the code in place, start your server by running:

cds watch

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

After running the application, select one or more employee records from the table. You'll notice that the Export Selected button is enabled only when records are selected. Clicking the button downloads an Excel file containing only the selected employees instead of the entire table.

 

 

 

 

Conclusion

What I liked most about this approach is that it keeps the implementation lightweight. Since the Excel file is generated in the browser using the SAPUI5 Spreadsheet library, there was no need to create a custom CAP action or write backend logic just for exporting data.

One thing I found useful was enabling Requires Selection for the custom action. Without it, users could click the button even when no rows were selected, resulting in unnecessary validation. Letting Fiori handle the button state provides a much better user experience.

Although this example exports employee data, the same approach can be used in almost any Fiori Elements application, such as Sales Orders, Purchase Orders, Expense Reports, or Products. If you've ever wanted to provide users with more control over what they export, this is a simple customization that's worth adding to your applications.

entry.title: Connecting SAP Commerce Cloud (CCv2) to SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition
entry.content:
• 1 Introduction
  • 2 SAP Commerce Cloud
  • 2.1 Backoffice Configuration
  • 3 SAP Application Router
  • 3.1 Introduction
  • 3.2 Architecture
  • 3.3 Implementation
  • 4 SAP API Management (APIM)
  • 4.1 Introduction
  • 4.2 Architecture
  • 4.3 SAP API Management Components
  • 4.4 Configuration of Cloud Connector
  • 4.5 Implementation
  • 5 Summary
  • 5.1 SAP API Management and Application Router - Comparison
  • 5.2 Conclusion

1       Introduction

If you use SAP Commerce Cloud (CCv2), you can leverage the SAP S/4HANA Order Management integration capabilities to integrate directly with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition. This enables order management through API-based communication between SAP Commerce Cloud and SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition.

This article describes the available integration options for connecting SAP Commerce Cloud to SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition using the SAP Connectivity service and Cloud Connector. The following approaches are covered:

  • Application Router on SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP)
  • SAP API Management on SAP Integration Suite

2       SAP Commerce Cloud

2.1      Backoffice Configuration

To configure the SAP Commerce Cloud Backoffice consumed destination for SAP S/4HANA Order Management, follow the steps in the integration implementation document. For more information, see SAP S/4HANA Order Management Integration Implementation

Note: Use the Application Router or SAP API Management hosting URL when you configure the Backoffice consumed destinations.

3       SAP Application Router

3.1      Introduction

The Application Router is a Node.js library used as a single point of entry to an enterprise application. The Application Router serves static content, authenticates users, rewrites URLs, and forwards requests to other microservices (acting as a proxy) while propagating user information.

For more information on Application Router and its implementation, see Application Router

3.2      Architecture

Process Flow
The following steps describe the process flow for connecting SAP Commerce Cloud to SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition via the Application Router:

  1. SAP Commerce Cloud Backoffice sends an HTTP request to the Cloud Foundry-hosted Application Router URL with a Bearer <token> in the Authorization header.
  2. Custom middleware (first in the pipeline) copies it to x-approuter-authorization.
  3. Application Router reads the token from x-approuter-authorization, validates it against SAP Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA), and matches the URL path against xs-app.json routes.
  4. The SAP BTP resolves the named destination to the actual backend URL.
  5. The SAP BTP Connectivity service tunnels the request through Cloud Connector to the SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition.
  6. SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition responds with the OData payload (sales order data or attachment).
  7. The Application Router forwards the response to SAP Commerce Cloud.    

3.3      Implementation

The Application Router runs as a Cloud Foundry application on SAP BTP. It is the central piece, handling authentication based on SAP Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA), destination resolution, and routing to the right SAP S/⁠4HANA Cloud Private Edition OData service.

Challenge: Limitation in the Backoffice Custom Header

SAP Application Router uses a special header called x-approuter-authorization to accept a pre-existing Bearer token and pass it through to the backend. This allows SAP Commerce Cloud to supply its own OAuth token for authorization of API calls.

The Backoffice in SAP Commerce Cloud does not support sending tokens in custom headers. It only uses the standard Authorization header.

Solution Proposal: A custom middleware that runs before the Application Router logic and transparently copies the Authorization header value into the x-approuter-authorization header.

 Solution Components

  • Server/Application Entry Point
    // server.js
'use strict';
const approuter = require('@sap/approuter');
const ar = approuter();
ar.start({
    extensions: [
        require('./middleware/tokenValidation')
    ]
});
​

The custom middleware is registered as an Application Router extension, the officially supported way to inject middleware into the Application Router lifecycle. When deployed on Cloud Foundry, the Cloud Foundry runtime calls npm start, which runs this file.

  • mta.yaml file
    This sample .yaml file is generated when you create an Application Router project.
_schema-version: "3.2"
ID: approuter
version: 1.0.0

modules:
- name: approuter-approuter
type: approuter.nodejs
path: approuter-approuter
parameters:
memory: 256M
disk-quota: 256M
properties:
LOG_LEVEL: debug
XS_APP_LOG_LEVEL: debug
requires:
- name: approuter-xsuaa
- name: approuter-destination
- name: approuter-connectivity

resources:
- name: approuter-xsuaa
type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
parameters:
service: xsuaa
service-plan: application
service-name: approuter-xsuaa-service
path: ./xs-security.json

- name: approuter-destination
type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
parameters:
service: destination
service-plan: lite

- name: approuter-connectivity
type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
parameters:
service: connectivity
service-plan: lite
​
  • Package.json file

    Add the file reference in package.json  scripts section so that it runs on npm start.

{
    "name": "approuter",
    "description": "description for approuter",
    "engines": {
        "node": ">=20"
    },
    "dependencies": {
        "@sap/approuter": "14.4.2"
    },
    "devDependencies": {
        "@sap/html5-repo-mock": "2.1.5"
    },
    "scripts": {
        "start": "node server.js",
        "start-local": "node node_modules/@sap/html5-repo-mock/index.js"
    }
}
  • The Custom Middleware

    // tokenValidation.js

    The tokenValidation.js file maps the Authorization header to the x-approuter-authorization header.

'use strict';

async function tokenValidationMiddleware(req, res, next) {
    if (req.headers['authorization'] && !req.headers['x-approuter-authorization']) {
        req.headers['x-approuter-authorization'] = req.headers['authorization'];
    }
    next();
}

module.exports = { insertMiddleware: { first: [tokenValidationMiddleware] } };

Custom Middleware Requirements

SAP Application Router looks for x-approuter-authorization to pick up a caller-supplied Bearer token. If this header is absent, the Application Router initiates its own OAuth flow (redirecting to SAP Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA) login page or returning 401).

The Backoffice in SAP Commerce Cloud can only send the Bearer token in the standard Authorization header. It has no mechanism to set custom headers.

Custom Middleware

  • Runs first, before any Application Router logic (insertMiddleware: { first: [...] }).
  • Checks if Authorization is present but x-approuter-authorization is not.
  • Copies the value across, so the Application Router sees the token it expects.
  • Calls next() to hand off to the normal Application Router pipeline.

No token is modified, no validation is done here — it's purely a header remapping step.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, ensure the following prerequisites are met:

  •  SAP BTP subaccount with Cloud Foundry environment enabled.
  •  Cloud Foundry CLI and MTA plug-in installed.
  •  Cloud Connector installed and linked to the SAP BTP subaccount.
  •  SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition virtual host/port mapped in Cloud Connector.
  •  SAP BTP Destinations created for each SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition OData service (OnPremise proxy type).
  • SAP Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA) service instance with appropriate scopes.
  •  SAP Commerce Cloud outbound credentials configured to call the Cloud Foundry Application Router URL with a valid Bearer token.

4       SAP API Management (APIM)

4.1      Introduction

The integration between SAP Commerce Cloud (CCv2) and SAP S/4HANA Order Management requires real-time, secure API access without custom middleware. SAP API Management provides a standardized and, handling OAuth 2.0 authentication, request routing, and security policies centrally.

For more information on SAP APIM, see Classic API Management.

4.2      Architecture

Process flow

The following steps describe the end-to-end process flow for the SAP API Management integration:

  1. SAP Commerce Cloud Backoffice sends an HTTP request to the SAP API Management Proxy URL with a Bearer <token> in the Authorization header.
  2. SAP API Management receives the request and runs the configured policies.
  3. SAP API Management resolves the target endpoint using the configured destination or target system and forwards the request.
  4. Cloud Connector establishes a secure tunnel between SAP BTP and the on-premise network hosting SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition.
  5. SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition processes the request and returns the required OData payload (for example, sales order data or attachments).

4.3   SAP API Management Components

The following table describes the key components of SAP API Management:

ComponentDescription
API ProviderDefines backend SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition connectivity, authentication, and discovery.
API ProxyExposes backend APIs securely with policy enforcement.
API ProductBundles APIs and defines access models such as OAuth or API Keys.
ApplicationRepresents the consuming application (CCv2) and generates credentials.

API Management Lifecycle (Design → Publish → Consume)

The following diagram illustrates the API Management lifecycle, from design through to consumption:

4.4      Configuration of Cloud Connector

SAP Cloud Connector enables SAP BTP applications to establish secure, encrypted connections to on-premise systems and remote services without exposing them directly to the internet.

For more information on the SAP Cloud Connector configuration, see Configuration of SAP Cloud Connector

4.5     Implementation


Create API Provider

To create an API provider, perform the following steps:

  1. In API Management, go to Configure and choose Create Provider. 
  2. On the Connection tab, select the type based on your system, and enter the host and port details.
  3. In the Catalog service settings, enter the following:
    • Path prefix
    • Service collection URL
    • Authentication type
    • Username
    • Password
  4. To verify the connection, choose Test Connection.
  5. Choose Save.

The API provider is created and available for use.

Create API Proxies

To create and activate an API proxy, perform the following steps:

  1. In API Management, go to Configure and choose APIs. 
  2. Choose Create and select the API Provider you previously configured.
  3. Choose Discover to load all backend APIs available in that Provider. Select the API you want to expose.
  4. Enter a name, title, and version for the new API proxy.
  5. Open the proxy to review or edit the details.
    Note: The Proxy Endpoint is the URL that clients call. The Target Endpoint shows the backend (API Provider) connection details and base URL.
  6. Choose Policies to add or edit policies such as security, transformation, and rate limits.
  7. Choose Save and Deploy to activate the proxy.

The proxy is activated and appears under Configure → APIs.

Create API Product

To create an API product and make it available for subscription, perform the following steps:

  1. In API Management, go to Engage and choose Products.
  2. Choose Create to start a new product.
  3. Enter a name, title, and optional description.
  4. On the APIs tab, choose Add and select the API proxies you want to include.
  5. Choose Publish to make the product available in the Developer Hub.

The API product is available for subscription in the Developer Hub.

Create Application

To create an application and subscribe to an API product, perform the following steps:

  1. In SAP Integration Suite, open the Developer Hub.
  2. Go to Applications and choose Create Application.
  3. Enter a name, description, and optional metadata.
  4. Go to the Subscriptions section and choose Add Subscription.
  5. Select the API Product you want the application to consume.
  6. Copy the generated credentials for use in your API calls. Use these credentials in tools like Bruno/Postman to call the API Proxy endpoint.
    Note: The credentials depend on the product's access model: an API key if the product requires API key authentication, or a client ID and client secret if it requires OAuth2.

Once subscribed, the application receives credentials based on the product’s access model.

5       Summary

5.1      SAP API Management and Application Router - Comparison

The following table compares SAP API Management and SAP Application Router across common integration scenarios.

 

Scenario

SAP API Management

Application Router

Internal M2M between trusted systems

Possible

Suitable

External API exposure to multiple consumers

Suitable

Possible with additional setup

SAP Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA) token already available at caller

Requires policy configuration

Suitable

Rate limiting / API analytics needed

Suitable

Requires additional tooling

Integration Suite already licensed

Suitable

Either works

No Integration Suite license

Requires procurement

Suitable

Cloud Foundry virtual host already provisioned

Suitable

Either works

Non-technical team managing changes

Possible via SAP Integration Suite UI

Possible via GitHub / BAS

Multiple backend services

One proxy per service

One Application Router, multiple routes

Create project from scratch

Higher setup effort upfront

Lower setup effort upfront

Version-controlled configuration

Requires custom setup

Built-in via GitHub

Enterprise API governance required

Suitable

Requires addition

 

5.2      Conclusion

Both SAP API Management and SAP Application Router are viable approaches for integrating SAP Commerce Cloud with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, each with its own strengths. The right choice depends on your existing landscape, licensing, and governance requirements. Customers already invested in Integration Suite will find SAP API Management the more natural fit, while those prioritizing simplicity and version-controlled configuration may prefer the Application Router approach. Both options are supported. Select the approach that best fits your technical landscape and project requirements.
