entry.title: BTP Trails, Part 1: SFLIGHT — From CDS Table to Secured API
entry.content:
This is the first installment of BTP Trails, a hands-on series documenting real build-and-deploy exercises on SAP Business Technology Platform — no idealized demos, just what actually happens (and what breaks) end to end.

Part 2 is already underway: standing up an SAP MCP Server in front of this same SFlight service so an AI agent can query flight data directly instead of a human hand-typing requests into Postman. This is the first published part of the series — future installments will be linked here as they go live.

Goal

Build a genuine CAP (Cloud Application Programming Model) service, backed by a real table in an SAP HANA Cloud HDI container, deployed to Cloud Foundry, and wired into SAP Integration Suite as a secured, managed API — end to end, against real BTP infrastructure, not a local simulation.

Model the data as a simplified version of the classic ABAP flight demo table SFLIGHT, dropping the ABAP MANDT client field, which carries no meaning in CAP or HANA Cloud.

Prerequisites

  • Cloud Foundry access to the subaccount. On a BTP trial, an org name i.e., “935b4163trial” and a default dev space are provisioned automatically, role collection “Subaccount Administrator” is automatically assigned.
  • SAP Business Application Studio (BAS) subscription, with role collection “Business_Application_Studio_Developer” assigned under Security → Users → Assign Role Collection in BTP Cockpit.
  • From the Service Marketplace, select the “SAP Hana Cloud” service and “Tools” subscription, with role collection “SAP HANA Cloud Administrator”

SAP Hana Cloud - Tools Subscription

  • Spin-up a SAP HANA Database instance using the SAP HANA Cloud application just deployed. Follow the following steps:
    1. Click “Create instance” and select “Configure manually”; Next Step
    2. Sign into Cloud Foundry environment with your BTP Account
    3. Create Database in “Cloud Foundry” runtime, your “dev” Space, provide an instance name i.e., “TVG_HDB’ and enter an Administrator Password; Next Step
    4. Next Step, and select “All IP addresses” as connections and ensure Cloud Connector is disabled; Next Step
    5. Next Step, Review and Create and Create Instance

SAP HANA DB Configuration Settings

  • From the Service Marketplace, select the “Integration Suite” application and assign role collections “Integration_Provisioner” and “PI_Integration_Developer”. Note: You cannot assign the PI_Integration_Developer role collection until step 6.3.
  • Postman (or another OAuth-capable REST client) installed, for testing purposes of the secured API.

When all is successfully deployed, the BTP Instances and Subscriptions page should look like the screenshot below.

Prerequisite Instances and Subscriptions

The End-to-End Flow

Everything below follows one straight line, start to finish:

  1. Model the CDS Entity — define the data structure in CAP's modeling language.
  2. Test Locally — validate the service against an in-memory database before touching the cloud.
  3. Bind to a HANA Cloud HDI Container — connect the project to a real, isolated database schema.
  4. Deploy Schema to HANA Cloud — generate the actual table from the CDS model.
  5. Deploy to Cloud Foundry — package and push the service to a public, running app.
  6. Wire the Service into Integration Suite — front it with a managed API artifact.
  7. Secure with OAuth — require a valid token on every call.
  8. Test in Postman — verify list, create, and single-record behavior end to end.

Let’s dive in…

1. Model the CDS Entity – the Source of Truth

  1. In BTP Cockpit, open the Business Application Studio subscription.
  2. Create a new Dev Space using the Full Stack Cloud Application template.
  3. Name it (e.g. TVG_DEV) and start it.
  4. In a BAS terminal enter the following 3 commands:
mkdir sflight-service
cd sflight-service
cds init​
  • Search and Open the newly created folder

This creates the standard CAP folder structure (db/, srv/, package.json, etc.).

1.1 Define the data model — db/schema.cds

Create under directory db/ a new file named schema.cds. Open the newly created file and paste the SFLIGHT table definition below.

namespace sap.demo.flights;

entity SFlight {
  key CarrID    : String(3);
  key ConnID    : String(4);
  key FlDate    : Date;
      Price     : Decimal(15,2);
      Currency  : String(5);
      PlaneType : String(20);
      SeatsMax  : Integer;
      SeatsOcc  : Integer;
}

Note: This mirrors the real ABAP SFLIGHT table, minus MANDT. The three key fields (CarrID, ConnID, FlDate) form a compound primary key — carrier + connection + flight date together uniquely identify a flight.

1.2 Expose it as a service — srv/service.cds

Similarly, in the folder srv/,  create a new file named service.cds, open it and copy and paste the service definition.

using sap.demo.flights from '../db/schema';
service FlightService {
  entity Flights as projection on flights.SFlight;
}

Note: This exposes the newly created schema as an OData V4 service named FlightService, with entity set Flights. No table exists anywhere yet — this is purely the model.

SFlight-Service CAP Model

2. Test Locally

Open a terminal window and run in BAS:

cds watch

By default, CAP spins up an in-memory SQLite database — no HANA DB needed yet. This is purely for validating the model and service definition.

CDS Watch - SQLite

Conduct a quick sanity check by opening a second terminal window and run:

curl http://localhost:4004/odata/v4/flight/Flights

If all is correct, this returns an empty value: [] array — confirming the service is live and the entity set is reachable. Remember, this is only the model and not an actual table no data can be found.

Curl against SQLite

3. Bind to a HANA Cloud HDI Container

Up until now we created and tested our CAP service against a fake in-memory database. Binding is the moment where we point the service to a persistent HANA DB where we can create the SFLIGHT table and store data in it. Lets unpack this a bit more as it tends to get confusing fast and/or is ofter misunderstood.

Picture three levels: the land — physical servers owned by a hyperscaler (AWS, in this case); SAP leases that land and builds a large facility on it — SAP HANA Cloud as a service; within that facility, your warehouse is a private building SAP provisions and leases out to you — your SAP HANA DB i.e., TVG_HDB. This warehouse walled off so no other SAP customer can access it, even though the facility itself sits on infrastructure SAP shares across many customers

The storage unit — an HDI container, i.e. TVG_HDC is a  single locked unit built inside your own warehouse. You don't strictly need that extra unit just to keep other customers out — the warehouse already does that — but it keeps multiple apps of your own from colliding with each other's tables as your project grows. Step 3.1 creates this container TVG_HDC. inside the warehouse TVG_HDB.

3.1 Create the HDI Container

In BTP Cockpit → Service Marketplace → SAP HANA Schemas & HDI Containers → create a new instance,  with plan hdi-shared and name it (e.g. TVG_HDIC).

This provisions an isolated, application-scoped schema (distinct from the HANA database instance (TVG_HDB)  itself, which represents the whole server and admin-level access).

HDI Container Creation on TVG_HDB

3.2 Ready the CAP Project for HANA and Bind to the Container

cds add hana
npm install
cf login -a https://api.cf.us10-003.hana.ondemand.com
cds bind -2 TVG_HDC

cds add hana registers HANA as a dependency — it updates package.json and .cdsrc.json to declare that this project needs @cap-js/hana, but doesn't install the package or provision anything on its own; npm install pulls in the actual dependency.

cds bind then connects your project to TVG_HDIC, the container you just created, saving its credentials locally under a named profile (used below as hybrid). The project now knows how to reach a real HANA Cloud schema — but that schema is still empty; nothing gets deployed until the next step.

Create HANA Dependency and Bind Project4. Deploy Schema to HANA Cloud

4.1 Deploy the Schema and Run Against Real HANA

Two commands are involved here, and the order matters — get it backwards and you'll hit a confusing error. First, deploy the schema:

cds deploy --to hana --profile hybrid

This is the step where the CDS model from Step 1 actually becomes a real table — it creates the .hdb table artifact inside your HDI container. Nothing exists in the database until this command runs.

Now start the service in hybrid mode, connecting to that real database instead of the in-memory one from Step 2:

cds watch --profile hybrid

In the screenshot below you can see that the we're now connecting to HANA and no longer SQLite.

CDS Watch against HANA DB, not SQLite

Running another curl check runs now against the real HANA DB.

curl http://localhost:4004/odata/v4/flight/Flights

 Again the result is an empty array as no data has been captured in the HANA DB table either.

4.2 Verify the table in SAP HANA Database Explorer (inside BAS)

Another way to see if a table was created on the HANA Database is to use the Database Explorer.

  • Use the hamburger menu: View → Command Palette → Database Explorer → SAP HANA: Open Database Explorer
  • Click + button to add an Instance, Instance Type: HDI Container and select the HANA Container i.e., TVG_HDI
  • Click Refresh few times for connection to be established
  • Browse to the "Tables", Select "SAP_DEMO_FLIGHTS_SFLIGHT" and confirm the schema/columns match SFlight.
  • Click Open Data to confirm the table itself is empty.

SAP Hana: Database Explorer

5. Deploy to Cloud Foundry

Up to this point, your CAP service has only run inside BAS — reachable from your own terminal, talking to a HANA container you bound to manually. That's fine for development, but it isn't a real, running application yet: nothing public-facing exists, and nothing is packaged the way a production deployment needs to be.

This step changes that. You'll package the project as an MTA (Multi-Target Application) — SAP's standard format for deploying multi-part projects (an app plus its database resources) to Cloud Foundry as one coordinated unit — and push it live. The result is a publicly reachable app with its own dedicated database, completely independent of your local BAS session.

5.1 Generate the Deployment Descriptor

cds add mta

This generates mta.yaml, a manifest describing everything Cloud Foundry needs to deploy: the app itself, and the database resources it depends on. Three pieces get defined:

  • sflight-service-srv — the actual Node.js application (your CAP service)
  • sflight-service-db-deployer — a helper module that deploys your schema into HANA as part of the deployment
  • sflight-service-db — a brand-new HDI container, provisioned fresh as part of this deployment

That third item is the one worth pausing on.

Note: MTA deployment provisions its own HDI container — separate from the one you bound to manually back in Step 3 (TVG_HDC in this walkthrough). This is intentional, not a bug: a real deployment shouldn't depend on a database container you happened to set up by hand during local testing. But it does mean your live app and your local hybrid testing end up writing to two different schemas. If you go looking for data afterward, make sure you're browsing the CF-deployed container in Database Explorer — not the one from Step 3, which the live app never touches.

5.2 Disable Built-in Production Auth

By default, CAP's production profile expects to authenticate requests itself, using XSUAA (SAP's auth service) — and it will refuse to start without it:

Error: Cannot find '@sap/xssec'

You don't want that here. Authentication for this project is going to be handled one layer up, at the Integration Suite gateway (Step 7) — so CAP's own auth needs to be turned off, or the app will crash on startup before Integration Suite ever gets involved. Add this to package.json file:

  "cds": {
    "requires": {
      "[production]": {
        "auth": {
          "kind": "dummy"
        }
      }
    }
  }

5.3 Build and Deploy

cf login
cf target -o <org> -s <space>
mbt build
cf deploy mta_archives/sflight-service_1.0.0.mtar

mbt build packages everything described in mta.yaml into a single deployable archive (.mtar). cf deploy then pushes that archive to Cloud Foundry — provisioning the new HDI container, deploying your schema into it, and starting the app, all in one operation.

Note: if mbt build fails with an npm ci EUSAGE error, your lock file is out of sync — run npm install once to resync package-lock.json, then rebuild.

Build and Deploy

Once deployed, confirm the app is actually live and publicly reachable:

 
curl https://<app-route>/odata/v4/flight/Flights

This should return value empty/empty array: [] (or real data, once records exist) — but now from the actual Cloud Foundry deployment, not your local BAS session.

Note: you'll find the exact app route in the deployment output printed during cf deploy — it's easy to miss among the other log lines, so look for it specifically once the deploy finishes (see screenshot below).

6. Wire the Service into Integration Suite

This step involves two separate BTP services working together, and it's worth understanding the difference before diving in — the terminology gets confusing otherwise, since both eventually point at the same backend.

The Destination lives in Connectivity, a BTP service entirely separate from Integration Suite. Think of a Destination as an address book entry: it just tells BTP "here's a URL, and here's how to reach it" — in this case, your Cloud Foundry app's route. Integration Suite doesn't own this piece; it only references it.

The API artifact lives in Integration Suite itself, and this is where the real work happens. Once deployed, it runs on Integration Suite's Integration Cell runtime — and that's not a one-time setup step you complete and move past. From this point through Step 8 (and beyond, once this is live), the Integration Cell is the actual server your requests hit. Postman, Claude, or any other client will never talk to your Cloud Foundry app directly again — every request goes through this runtime first, which enforces OAuth, applies any routing/policy logic, and only then forwards the request on to your CAP service using the Destination's address.

In short: the Destination is a pointer, and the API artifact + Integration Cell is the actual gateway standing in front of your app.

6.1 Create a BTP Destination

BTP Cockpit → Connectivity → Destinations → New Destination:

  • URL: the deployed app's route + relative path (e.g. https://<app-route>/odata/v4/flight)
  • Proxy Type: Internet
  • Authentication: NoAuthentication (auth is handled at the gateway, not the destination)
  • Label: IntegrationCell.Include = true

BTP Destination Definition

6.2 Generate an accurate OpenAPI spec directly from CAP

Rather than hand-writing an OpenAPI spec and risking it drifting out of sync with the real service, let CAP generate one straight from your live model:

cds compile srv --to openapi > sflight-openapi.json

This gives you a spec whose entity names, field types, and — critically — the exact key-predicate syntax for the compound key (CarrID, ConnID, FlDate) all come directly from your actual CDS definitions, rather than something you'd have to get right by hand.

One edit is actually required before this is ready to import: the paths need to be relative to Destination + Relative URL, not repeat the entity name. As generated, CAP writes /Flights and /Flights(CarrID=...) — but since the Destination will already carry that segment, these need to become / and /(CarrID=...) instead. Skipping this causes the exact double-slash duplication bug covered in the Troubleshooting Log.

Rather than editing the JSON by hand, create a JavaScript file in your BAS project called "fix-openapi-paths.js" and add the following code:

// fix-openapi-paths.js
const fs = require('fs');
const file = process.argv[2] || 'sflight-openapi.json';
const spec = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8'));

const newPaths = {};
for (const [path, def] of Object.entries(spec.paths)) {
  if (path === '/$batch') continue; // drop batch, operates at service root
  const newPath = path.replace(/^\/Flights/, '') || '/';
  newPaths[newPath] = def;
}
spec.paths = newPaths;

fs.writeFileSync(file, JSON.stringify(spec, null, 2));
console.log('Done. Paths now:', Object.keys(spec.paths));

Then run following command:

node fix-openapi-paths.js sflight-openapi.json

This makes the necessary changes to the JSON file which we will need when we define the API artifact in the following step.

Optional polish, not required for functionality: CAP leaves info.title, info.description, and info.version as placeholder text — feel free to fill these in for a nicer-looking artifact in the Integration Suite portal, but it costs nothing to skip. Same goes for servers[0].url — the import wizard's own Destination and Relative URL fields drive actual routing, so this value is mostly cosmetic.

Validate the result before moving on:

node -e "JSON.parse(require('fs').readFileSync('sflight-openapi.json'))" && echo "Valid JSON"

6.3 Import as an API Artifact

Everything so far has been preparation — the Destination points at your app, and the OpenAPI spec describes its shape. This step is where those two pieces actually come together into a live, callable API artifact inside Integration Suite. After opening the Integration Suite, perform the following preparation steps:

  1. Create and activate capability with API Modelling, select option "Manage APIs". Ensure options "API Modelling" and "Developer Hub" are selected.
  2. Select Settings → Runtimes → Integration Cell → Activate
  3. Go to BTP Cockpit and assign role collection "PI_Integration_Developer” to your user. Note: you need to log off/on from Integration Suite to get the API design capabilities activated for your user.

With this done, start by creating an Integration Package — a container that groups related artifacts together. Since this series will eventually include both an API artifact and an MCP Server artifact, put them in the same package from the start (e.g., TVG_PCK) rather than scattering them across separate ones.

Inside that package, go to the Artifacts tab → Add → API, and work through the import wizard:

1. Runtime Profile: Integration Cell

This tells Integration Suite which underlying runtime will actually host and serve this artifact. Integration Cell is what this entire walkthrough runs on, so select it here and click Next.

2. Method: URL or Specification

Integration Suite offers a few ways to define an API artifact — you could describe one manually, or point at an existing API definition. Since you already have an accurate, CAP-generated OpenAPI spec, choose this option so the wizard builds the artifact directly from that file rather than asking you to redefine everything by hand.

3. API Details

This is where the pieces you've built in the last two steps get wired together:

  • Upload → File: sflight-openapi.json — the spec you generated and fixed with the script in Step 6.2.
  • Type: the Destination you created earlier (e.g. TVG_DST) — this tells the artifact which backend to actually forward requests to.
  • Target → Relative URL: /Flights — this is the piece that completes the routing, appending the entity set name on top of the Destination's service-root URL. (This is also the field that has to line up with the path edits made in Step 6.2 — get one without the other and you're back to the duplicated-segment error.)
  • Service Type: REST
  • API Base Path: /sflight — this becomes the public-facing prefix for every call to this artifact, e.g. https://<api-host>/sflight.
  • Runtime Profile: Integration Cell (confirming the same choice from step 1).

Once you've filled these in and deployed, this artifact becomes the actual gateway your client calls — no longer talking to your Cloud Foundry app directly, but through this managed, policy-enforced layer instead.

7. Secure with OAuth

Every API artifact deployed to Integration Cell automatically enforces OAuth authentication — this cannot (and should not) be disabled. Any request without a valid Bearer token is rejected outright.

This enforcement is implemented through two policies, both built into the artifact and applied by Integration Suite on every incoming request:

  • Authentication policy — verifies that a token is present at all.
  • Authorization policy — verifies that the token's scope claim includes API.invoke. A token that lacks this specific scope is rejected exactly as if no token had been provided.

Authorization and Authentication Policies

Before Postman (or any other client) can call the API, it therefore needs a way to obtain a token that satisfies both checks — a token issued by an OAuth client that Integration Suite trusts, carrying the API.invoke scope. The rest of this step covers how to provision that client and use it to obtain a token.

The mechanism for provisioning a trusted OAuth client is a specific BTP service instance. Creating this instance has nothing to do with running integration flows — its sole relevant purpose here is that SAP issues a matching OAuth client as a byproduct of its creation.

7.1 BTP Instance Configuration

1. Create the service instance:

In BTP Cockpit → your subaccount → Instances and Subscriptions → Create:

  • Service: SAP Process Integration Runtime
  • Plan: integration-flow — this specific plan matters. It bundles the roles ESBMessaging.send and API.invoke, which is what makes the resulting OAuth client actually usable for this purpose. The other, api, looks similar but only grants design-time roles — an OAuth client created under that plan will not produce a token that Integration Suite accepts here.
  • Name it (e.g. matching your project's naming convention) and create it i.e., TVG_PIR.

2. Generate a service key:

Click into the instance you just created → Service Keys tab → Create. Give the key a name and confirm i.e, TVG_KEY.

This generates a JSON credentials file containing the actual clientid, clientsecret, and token URL (url) for the OAuth client SAP provisioned alongside the instance. You'll use these three values directly in Postman's OAuth 2.0 configuration in the next step.

OAuth Key

7.2 Configure Postman to obtain a Token

1. Set the Authorization type and Grant Type:

In Postman, open the requests Authorization tab, set Type to OAuth 2.0, then set Grant Type to Client Credentials. This tells Postman there's no human login involved — just a direct exchange of client ID and secret for a token, which is what a machine-to-machine call like this needs. Postman's default Grant Type, Authorization Code, expects a browser login redirect instead and will fail with Invalid host for auth URL if left unchanged.

Step 2 — Enter the service key's credentials:

From the JSON service key generated in the previous step, copy:

  • clientid → Postman's Client ID field
  • clientsecret → Postman's Client Secret field
  • url (the token endpoint) → Postman's Access Token URL field

Click Get New Access Token.

Step 3 — Confirm the token is attached:

Postman fetches a token from that URL and attaches it as an Authorization: Bearer <token> header on the request. This is the exact token Step 8's calls will use — confirm it appears before moving on.

Postman OAuth2.0 Configuration

8. Test in Postman

Everything up to this point has been infrastructure and configuration — a CDS model, a real HANA table, a Cloud Foundry deployment, a Destination, an OAuth-secured gateway. None of it has actually proven anything yet. This is the moment that changes: the first real request, from a real client, through the full chain you just built.

If this works, it means every layer is doing its job at once — CAP is serving data from a genuine HANA Cloud table, Integration Suite is correctly routing and rewriting the request, and OAuth is gating access exactly as intended. One broken link anywhere in that chain, and this is where it would show up.

8.1 Create a Flight

POST: https://<api-artifact-host>/sflight

Authorization: OAuth 2.0 / Bearer <token>

Body: Raw (json)

{
  "CarrID": "AA",
  "ConnID": "0017",
  "FlDate": "2011-02-17",
  "Price": 450.00,
  "Currency": "USD",
  "PlaneType": "747",
  "SeatsMax": 300,
  "SeatsOcc": 120
}

And hit the send button, if all is ok we should be able to create an entry in the HANA DB table in the SFLIGHT container.

Postman POST Event Response

8.2 Retrieve a Flight

GET: https://<api-artifact-host>/sflight

Authorization: OAuth 2.0 / Bearer <token>

And the results should retrieve the flight details we created in previous step.

Postman GET Response

Lets see if we can also locate the newly created flight record in the SAP HANA DB using the Database Explorer we described in paragraph 4.2. Per the screenshot below, you should be able to see the single record we created during the Postman POST event.

Record View in HANA DB

Troubleshooting Log

Grouped by phase, so you can jump to where you're stuck rather than scanning one long list.

Local CAP Development

Symptom Cause Fix
mbt build fails with npm error could not determine executable to run on the npx cds build --production step@SAP/cds-dk isn't installed globally — common in a fresh BAS Dev Space, since nothing carries over from a previous onenpm install -g @SAP/cds-dk, confirm with cds --version, then rebuild
Cannot find module '@cap-js/hana' on cds watch --profile hybridcds add hana configures HANA support but doesn't install the dependencynpm install
invalid table name: Could not find table/view ... in hybrid modeSchema was never deployed to the bound HDI containercds deploy --to hana --profile hybrid before cds watch --profile hybrid, not after

Cloud Foundry Build & Deploy

Symptom Cause Fix
Error: Cannot find '@sap/xssec' on Cloud Foundry startupProduction profile defaults to JWT auth, requiring an XSUAA bindingSet cds.requires.[production].auth.kind to "dummy" in package.json — auth is handled at the Integration Suite gateway instead
mbt build fails with an npm ci EUSAGE errorpackage-lock.json is out of syncnpm install once to resync, then rebuild
cf deploy fails: "No deployment descriptor with name mtad.yaml was found"Run bare, without pointing at the built .mtar archivecf deploy mta_archives/<name>_<version>.mtar — confirm the file exists first with ls mta_archives/
cf deploy / cf apps fails repeatedly: "Authentication has expired"CF CLI session timed outcf login -a <endpoint> then cf target -o <org> -s <space>, then retry
App returns a raw Cloud Foundry 404 — Requested route (...) does not exist — even though the route was previously workingThe app itself was stopped (trial CF apps can be auto-stopped after inactivity, distinct from the route being deleted)cf apps to confirm state, then cf start <app-name> if it shows stopped / web:0/1
curl .../Flights returns 500, CF logs show TimeoutError: ResourceRequest timed out from the connection poolThe HANA Cloud instance itself was stopped (same trial auto-stop pattern, but at the database layer)BTP Cockpit → Instances and Subscriptions → find the HANA Cloud instance → Start/Resume, wait a few minutes, retry
POST succeeded but the new row is missing in Database ExplorerBrowsing the old HDI container used for local hybrid testing, not the new one the CF deployment's MTA db-deployer createdConnect Database Explorer to the CF-deployed container specifically, and check the data preview tab, not just Definition

Integration Suite Setup (Capabilities, Roles, Subscription)

Symptom Cause Fix
Integration Suite missing entirely from Instances and SubscriptionsBTP trial auto-unsubscribes Integration Suite after a period of inactivityRe-subscribe and rebuild Destination, API artifact, and OAuth wiring from scratch — the CAP app and HANA Cloud DB are unaffected, since they're separate subscriptions
Integration Suite home screen shows only Home/Settings, even after subscribingCapabilities aren't activated by default on subscribe — it's a separate stepBTP Cockpit → Boosters → "Enable Integration Suite" → select Manage APIs (not "Build Integration Scenarios," which is for Cloud Integration/iFlows and isn't needed here)
Design/Monitor tiles still don't appear, even after capabilities show fully activatedMissing the PI_Integration_Developer role collection — not obviously named for what it unlocks; two other API-sounding roles look like the fix but aren't sufficient aloneSecurity → Users → your user → Role Collections → assign PI_Integration_Developer, then fully log out/in of Integration Suite (a plain refresh isn't enough)

API Artifact Creation & OpenAPI Import

Symptom Cause Fix
Resource not found for the segment 'flights'OData entity set names are case-sensitive; Relative URL / API Base Path casing didn't matchMatch casing exactly (Flights, capital F) in both the Destination's Relative URL and the API Base Path
Integration Suite's Add API wizard rejects the spec: "An error occurred while validating the OpenAPI specification due to some invalid or missing fields"A scripted path rename (/Flights → /) can accidentally strip the leading slash from the compound-key path, leaving something like (CarrID=...) instead of /(CarrID=...) — invalid per the OpenAPI spec. An empty info.version string can also fail validation.Confirm every path key still starts with / after any scripted edit; make sure info.title/description/version are filled in, non-empty values
API artifact deploys, but Monitor shows "Error" / "The API is not operational"Observed as one-off trial flakiness — config checked out correctly, and a plain retry succeeded with no changes madeTry a plain retry of Deploy before deep-diving into config — Integration Suite on trial has shown intermittent deploy flakiness that resolves on its own
Deployed API artifact sits in "Starting" — or cycles to "Stopping" without completing — for 20+ minutes, no errors anywhereMost likely thin compute capacity on the trial tier, not a config problemConfirm runtime health (Settings → Runtimes) and entitlement quota aren't the actual cause, then be prepared to simply wait — one case here resolved cleanly overnight

Routing: Destination + Relative URL Concatenation

Symptom Cause Fix
Entity "FlightService.Flights" has 3 keys. Only N were provided or Invalid resource path, on every call through the API artifact, even with a correctly configured destination and freshly re-imported artifactThe Destination URL already ended in the entity set name (/Flights). Relative URL is a required field and can never be blank — its minimum is a single / — so it always contributes at least one extra character on top of a Destination that's already complete, producing a duplicated segment or trailing slash that CAP's OData parser rejectsMove the entity set segment out of the Destination and into Relative URL instead: trim the Destination back to the service root (.../odata/v4/flight) and set Relative URL to /Flights. The matched root resource (/) contributes nothing extra, so the concatenation resolves cleanly
artifactNotFound on a compound-key path, despite correct Resources tab registrationThis gateway's route matcher likely doesn't reliably support multiple placeholders combined in a single path segmentUse $filter on the list endpoint as the dependable fallback for single-record reads, rather than the compound-key path directly

OAuth

Symptom Cause Fix
Service key JSON pasted into Postman has no clientid/clientsecret fields — just hdi_user, hdi_password, schema, etc.Generated from the HDI container binding instead of the Process Integration Runtime instance — the two look similarly "official" but serve completely different purposesGenerate the service key specifically from the Process Integration Runtime instance, plan integration-flow (not api, which only grants design-time roles and won't produce a usable token)

Key Takeaways

  • CAP's cds compile srv --to openapi produces a far more reliable OpenAPI spec than hand-writing one, since it reflects the actual live service definition — entity names, field types, and key-predicate syntax all come from the real model.
  • A BTP Destination's URL and an API artifact's Relative URL concatenate literally; trailing/leading slashes and path segment casing on either side can silently break specific calls even when others succeed.
  • OAuth scopes for Integration Cell API artifacts depend on the specific plan of the backing service instance — Process Integration Runtime, plan integration-flow, not api.
  • Each MTA deployment to Cloud Foundry that includes a HANA resource provisions its own HDI container — it's easy to end up debugging against a stale container left over from earlier local development.
  • BTP trial resources are more disposable than they feel. Over the course of building this series, the working trial subaccount changed three separate times, the Integration Suite subscription was fully removed once, and both the HANA Cloud instance and the Cloud Foundry app were independently auto-stopped after periods of inactivity — each producing a different, initially confusing symptom (missing subscription, connection timeout, raw CF 404) that traced back to the same root cause: trial infrastructure winding itself down when unused. If something that worked yesterday suddenly doesn't, checking whether the underlying instance/app/ subscription is still actually running is a good first move, before assuming something in your own config broke.
  • Capability activation and role collection assignment are two separate gates in Integration Suite, both required before Design/Monitor tiles even appear — neither is obviously named for what it unlocks, so a "successfully completed" booster run isn't the whole story.
  • Integration Suite on trial has shown occasional flakiness on deploy and startup that resolves with a plain retry or a wait, without any actual config being wrong — worth trying before assuming a real bug.

Coming Up in Part 2

There's now a real, query-able flight dataset sitting behind a secured, production-grade API — built the hard way, with every gotcha documented along the way. Which raises the obvious next question: why should a human be the one typing requests into Postman?

Part 2 of BTP Trails answers that. It stands up an SAP MCP Server in front of this same SFlight service — so instead of you crafting OData queries by hand, Claude does it. Ask "which airline has the most flights?" in plain English, and watch an AI agent reach through Integration Suite, hit the live API you just built, and answer from real data.

entry.title: SAP UX Q3/2026 Update – Part 9: AI, AI, but not only! UI Design and Technology for Web and Mobile
entry.content:
This ninth and last post in my series gives an overview innovations in our UI tools and technologies, making it ever easier to design, build and integrate UIs, for both web and mobile applications. The compositional design system is powering AI-native engagement layer experiences in Joule Work. AI is making it much easier to design and code: we have a large number of innovations there, with MCP server enhancements and plug-ins for Claude Code and GitHub Copilot, as well as providing the AI-powered Project Accelerator from SAP Fiori tools for ABAP too. But that’s not all, we’ve also invested in usability, performance and extensibility. We’ve also been looking at mobile development, with enhancements for web apps on mobile phones, as well as support for embedding AI into apps built with the mobile development kit.

Joule can also be seen as a technology for delivering a great user experience. To find out about recent innovations there, as well as for central entry points and services, have a look at this post, which also contains links to all the other parts of the series:

  • SAP UX Q3/2026 Update – Part 1: AI, Joule, Mobile, SAP Build Work Zone.

In case you missed them, do have a look at my previous posts covering design and technology news, since what I mention here builds partly on what came before:

  • SAP UX Q3/2025 Update – Part 7: UI Design and Technology for Web and Mobile.
  • SAP User Experience Q1/2026 Update – Part 9: UI Design and Technology for Web and Mobile – this post introduced our MCP servers for SAPUI5 and SAP Fiori elements.

First, we’ll have a look at news for creating web UIs, before looking at what’s new for mobile design and development.

I’ve compiled the news into these sections:

  • AI Design Innovations
  • AI for UI5
  • AI for SAP Fiori tools
  • Extensibility news
  • Further news for SAPUI5 and SAP Fiori elements
  • Mobile optimized for Web
  • Mobile app development news

 

AI Design Innovations

The big news for SAP Design is our work on the compositional design system which powers Joule Work and its new engagement layer experiences, which complement existing application experiences.

Beyond that, we have introduced AI skills for designers of application experiences.

Compositional Design System for Joule Work

With Joule Work we are introducing entirely new, AI-native user experiences. We call these engagement layer experiences, which complements existing application experiences.

Figure 1: The compositional design system for AI-generated UIs. Alt Text: image depicting schematically “The compositional design system” on the left with a line linking it to a UI wireframe on the right depicted “Generated user interface”.

At the heart of Joule Work are Spaces: dynamically composed workspaces generated based on the user’s intent and context. Figure 2 shows examples of what such generated UIs looks like.

Figure 2: Examples of AI-generated UIs in Joule Work Spaces. Alt Text: Two images, one showing a desktop with a Space containing information on a return order from customer BikePros, showing status data as text, numbers and chards, the other showing a subset of the same information on a mobile phone screen.

If you want to have a look at how we are designing these new experiences, and see how we are evolving the SAP Design System for AI-driven UX, look here:

  • Designing the Autonomous Enterprise.
  • The Compositional Design System.
  • AI and Design.

If you want more information about the Joule Work user experience, have a look at my blog post:

  • SAP UX Update: The New Joule Work Engagement Layer Experiences

Skills for Designing SAP Fiori Applications

We have recently introduced several AI skills for designers using Figma. The highlight is the skill for the SAP Fiori guidelines, for web and for iOS, but we also have introduced two for the Theme Designer.

SAP Fiori guidelines design skill: Use this skill when designing, building, or reviewing SAP Fiori applications, implementing SAPUI5 or UI5 Web Components, working with SAP enterprise UX patterns, or needing guidance on buttons, forms, tables, object pages, list reports, navigation, messaging, colors, typography, accessibility, AI/Joule integration, or any SAP Fiori UI element.

  • SAP Fiori guidelines design skill in SAP AI skills library

SAP Fiori for iOS design skill: Converts Figma designs from the SAP Fiori iOS UI Kit into correct SwiftUI prototype code with Fiori color tokens, typography, animations, and component guidelines. Use this skill when a designer provides a Figma node ID or component name and wants working SwiftUI code, when asking which Fiori iOS component to use, when mapping Figma variants to SwiftUI, or when adding animations and state transitions to iOS prototypes.

  • SAP Fiori for iOS design skill in SAP AI skills library

Theme Designer skills: we have introduced these two skills, one for providing guidance on usng tokens from the design system, the other providing help based on the documentation:

  • UI Theme Designer Design Tokens skill
  • UI Theme Designer Help skill

 

AI for UI5

This last half year our engineers have been focusing on AI: how can we enable you to create apps faster and better with the help of AI. The main investments have been in providing or improving our MCP servers, providing plug-ins to enable agents, and bringing AI to ABAP development too.

UI5 Plugins for Coding Agents (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot)

In April we introduced the UI plugins for Claude. These have since been generalized, so that they are not limited to Claude Code, and renamed to “UI5 Plugins for Coding Agents”, supporting GitHub Copilot in addition to Claude Code.

Figure 3: Alt Text: Image with Claude and GitHub icons above the text “UI5 Plugins for Coding Agents” – “New Release” – “Start your UI5 journey with Copilot and Claude”.

What can you do with these plugins? Let’s have a look…

UI5 Plugin — Your UI5 Development Companion

The UI5 plugin equips coding agents with deep knowledge of the SAPUI5 and OpenUI5 ecosystem. It helps you with the following tasks:

  • Create new UI5 projects: Create scaffolded project structures based on best practices without any manual setup.
  • Detect and fix UI5-specific errors: Claude understands UI5 linting rules and applies fixes based on the official guidelines.
  • Access UI5 API documentation: Get accurate, framework-aware answers about controls, modules, events, and APIs instead of generic JavaScript suggestions.

The UI5 plugin was recently enhanced with these three new skills, and also made available for GitHub Copilot:

  • UI Integration Cards: UI Integration Cards have very specific rules around data placement, binding syntax, and manifest structure. This new skill encodes those rules so the agent can get cards right without trial and error.
  • OPA5 integration tests: Writing reliable OPA5 tests requires knowing the actual control tree of the running app — something a coding agent can't derive from source alone. This skill bridges that gap. It also covers initial test configuration, multi-view setups, page object organization, and teardown patterns.
  • UI5 Tables: This skill helps agents get tables right, by enforcing essential patterns and production-ready handling for performance, personalization, drag and drop, and data type alignment.

UI5 TypeScript Conversion plugin — Migrate to TypeScript with Confidence
Migrating a JavaScript UI5 project to TypeScript can be tricky. Generic AI tools often handle the required transformations incorrectly. The UI5 TypeScript Conversion plugin provides coding agents with a step-by-step conversion playbook.

UI5 Modernization Plugin: ​Keeping your SAPUI5 or OpenUI5 app up to date just got easier. The new UI5 Modernization Plugin automates the most time-consuming parts of app modernization: replacing deprecated APIs, eliminating global namespaces, updating manifest.json and Component.js, and getting your app ready for Content Security Policy compliance. The plugin is available as a Claude Code plugin and in the GitHub Copilot marketplace.

Find out more here:

  • Introducing UI5 Plugins for Claude: AI-Powered Development for SAPUI5 and OpenUI5
  • UI5 Plugins for Coding Agents: Now Supporting GitHub Copilot (with details on the three recently added skills decribed above)
  • Introducing the UI5 Modernization Plugin: Modernize Your OpenUI5/SAPUI5 App in Hours, Not Weeks

UI5 MCP Server News

If you don’t want to use the above UI5 Modernization Plugin, you can use the UI5 MCP server with GitHub Copilot. Find out more here:

The agent does most of the work, and you can focus on code review.https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-sap/how-to-migrate-ui5-projects-to-the-latest-ui5-best-practices/ba-p/14340388

This blog post focuses on how the UI5 MCP server can support you in migrating your UI5 project easily to the latest best practices with the help of GitHub Copilot Coding Agent. Migrate your project.

ABAP AI in SAP Joule for Developers

Although this is not directly UI related, a good user experience of course relies on good back-end services, which are often built with ABAP. Hence I’d like to mention that ABAP AI capabilities including agentic capabilities is now offered as a service across SAP BTP ABAP Environment, SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, and SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition for releases 2021 and higher. Find out more here:

  • SAP Joule for Developers, ABAP AI capabilities including agentic capabilities is now available!

 

AI for SAP Fiori Tools

Project Accelerator for ABAP Cloud

The Project Accelerator supports rapid prototyping with AI, based on images and/or a requirements description. It has been available for CAP (SAP Cloud Application Programming Model) since 2024, where it can generate database tables, OData services and UIs from a sketch or a description.

Now, you have the same power for ABAP development following the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) – for SAP Business AI Platform as well as for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition.

Figure 4: SAP Fiori tools project accelerator. Alt Text: three images on the left: a high-fidelity Figma model, a lower fidelity screenshot, and a sketch on paper, with an pointy bracket leading to the text “Use SAP Fiori tools project accelerator to generate the app”. On the right an extract of the accelerator’s screen, showing a thumbnail of an uploaded image.

Find out more here:

  • Develop RAP-Based SAP Fiori Applications in Minutes with SAP Fiori Tools AI Project Accelerator

MCP Server and Skills for SAP Fiori

MCP News for SAP Fiori

AI-Chat in SAP Business Application Studio for SAP Fiori: SAP Business Application Studio now includes an AI Chat capability that you can use for MCP-supported AI-driven SAP Fiori development directly from the browser. 

Installing the MCP server locally: For local development, the MCP server for SAP Fiori is now available through the MCP registry on GitHub. You can also install it as a Claude plugin, together with our new skills (more on that below).

Full Stack AI-Driven Development in VS Code:  The MCP server for SAP Fiori pairs with the new ABAP MCP server, which is part of the ABAP development tools for Visual Studio Code. Together, the two bridge the gap between backend ABAP services and the SAP Fiori frontend, enabling a true fullstack AI-driven development experience from within VS Code. For more details, watch Christoph Gollmick’s ABAPConf presentation:

  • AI-Powered Full-Stack Dev with SAP’s MCP Servers for ABAP & SAP Fiori

Skills for SAP Fiori

We have now published the first set of skills that complement the MCP server for SAP Fiori:

  • SAP Fiori app development: Guides the creation and modification of SAP Fiori elements applications in CAP and standalone projects
  • Analytical chart: Adds an analytical chart and table hybrid to a List Report, supporting CAP and ABAP RAP (OData V4)
  • Visual filter: Adds chart-based visual filters to the filter bar or value help in SAP Fiori elements applications
  • Create CLI: Runs and automates the CLI for generating, converting, and managing Fiori projects
  • ESLint plug-in: Configures, migrates, or runs ESLint with the ESLint plugin for SAP Fiori tools in SAP Fiori projects.

 

Extensibility for Key Users and Developers

Key User Adaptation and Transition to Developer Extensibility

Apparently, many customers are still not aware of all the great options we provide for users to adapt the UI without needing to ask IT administrators for support.

A key user is a business expert who is authorized to make changes on behalf of other users — for example a team member who is interested in technology. The goal of key user extensibility is to empower business users to be able to adapt their working environment to suit their needs, without having to rely on system administrators.

This nice overview blog post explains how to use it, and also explains how you can easily transition from key user extensibility to developer extensibility:

  • Key User Adaptation: Powerful New Features & Seamless Transition to Developer Extensibility.

Have a look at this video to see it in action:

  • Video: Extending SAP Fiori Object Pages with Adapt UI (13:26 min.)

Adapting UIs for Specific User Roles now available on SAP Business AI Platform

Great news for BTP developers! The SAPUI5 Flexibility features described in this blog post are now available on the SAP BTP Cloud Foundry environment starting with UI5 version 1.146:

  • SAPUI5 Flexibility: Adapting UIs for Specific User Roles.

New Name: UI5 Flexibility Service

We have renamed „UI5 flexibility for key users“ to „UI flexibility service”.

We did this because we had introduced end user personalization capabilities in addition to key user adaptation, so the name became rather misleading. Find out more in this blog post:

  • More Power, New Name: The UI Flexibility Service Explained

 

Further News for UI5 and SAP Fiori elements

Developing apps with modern concepts: guidance for developers

Developers often need to balance development efficiency, maintenance costs, and design flexibility when building enterprise-ready applications with SAP Fiori elements and freestyle SAPUI5. With the introduction of Building Blocks a while ago we offer a lot of flexibility, so that you can choose the approach that fits your needs best. To help you make the right decision, we have created this guidance for you:

  • Developing Apps with Modern Concepts: Guidance for Developers

The SAP Fiori development portal that I introduced in my previous post is your entry point for discovering the various options in detail and starting your development. This is described in this series of blog posts in more detail:

  • Introducing the SAP Fiori Development Portal: Your Gateway to Rapid SAP Fiori App Creation (1 of 6).

TypeScript 6 and 7 – What UI5 TypeScript developers need to know in 2026

TypeScript is going through its biggest transition in years - and if you build UI5 applications with TypeScript, here we have all the details you need to know.

Read about it in this blog post.

Usability Improvements in SAP Fiori Tools

The 2603 release brought several usability improvements:

  • Direct navigation to source in the manifest gives developers a more transparent editing experience.
  • New walkthrough for getting started makes novice developers more productive more quickly (see Figure 5).
  • Import key user changes into an Adaptation Project and keep your edits (as already described above in the section on Extensibility).

Figure 5: Walkthrough for SAP Fiori tools. Alt Text: Image of the welcome screen, with a list of topics on the left, with “What is SAP Fiori Tools?” selected. On the right a description text with five bullet points.

Learn more about these improvements here:

  • SAP Fiori Tools 2603 Update: RAP Project Accelerator, Walkthrough, Adaptation Improvements, and More

Renovations and Performance Improvements in SAP Fiori Tools

The latest release of SAP Fiori tools brings quite a few renovations and performance improvements. Highlights are:

  • Moving from CommonJS to ECMAScript Modules
  • ESLint 10 upgrade
  • 80% faster extension startup.

Have a look at these in more detail, along with another six smaller improvements:

  • SAP Fiori Tools 2607 Update: Skills, Fullstack AI Development, and Performance

 

Mobile optimized for Web

The SAP Fiori elements team has been working on optimizing the user experience of web-based SAP Fiori elements apps for mobile phone users. If you use SAP Joule mobile app (formerly SAP Mobile Start), it gives you a list of all SAP applications available to you – both native mobile apps as well as web apps, such as those from SAP S/4HANA Cloud. Tapping on one of these web apps will launch the app directly, so as a user you don’t notice that it is running in a browser.

This is currently available to customers via this Early Adopter Care (EAC) program. If you are interested, do sign up, registration ends November 28, 2026.

As you can see in Figure 6, the layout for lists and object pages is more intuitive than before.

Figure 6: SAP Fiori elements mobile phone optimization (EAC), with a list report on the left, an object page on the right. Alt Text: two mobile phone images for the app Manage Product Costing, the list showing three entries each with product ID, name, category, supplier and price shown. The object page shows the header and two tabs, with General Information selected, showing the Order Details section and part of the Admin Data section.

Re-imagining filters on mobile using natural language

Filter bars are great on a desktop, but using them on a mobile phone is a real challenge. Now that we have natural language AI-assisted Easy Filters, perhaps we can use natural language to get a much better filtering experience on mobile phones? This is precisely what our engineering teams are looking into (Figure 6).

Figure 7: Traditional filter bar on a mobile phone compared to AI-powered natural language filter. Alt Text: two mobile phone screens, on the left a list of filter names to select, on the right an Easy Filter text entry field above buttons “Recent” and “Favorites”.

Find out more here, and sign up for the Early Adopter Care program if you want to try it out and give us feedback:

  • Reimagining Filters on Mobile: A Natural Language Approach in SAP Fiori Elements

 

Mobile App Development News

SAP Fiori for Android and SAP Fiori for iOS 26.4 Release Updates

The SAP BTP SDK for iOS and the SAP BTP SDK for Android have shipped their 26.4 releases, each containing several feature enhancements to these components:

  • List Picker Form Cell (iOS and Android)
  • Switch Form Cell (iOS and Android)
  • Step Progress Indicator (Android only)
  • Hyperlinked Text Style (Android only)

Find out more here:

  • What’s New for SAP BTP SDK for iOS 26.4
  • What’s New for SAP BTP SDK for Android 26.4

Mobile development kit (MDK)

The last two releases have brought some nice new features, with two important ones for enabling embedded AI in mobile apps. In the following sections I’d like to highlight these:

  • Contact Cell control enhancements
  • AI Notice Form Cell Control
  • AI Feedback Form Cell Control
  • Stepper Form Cell Control
  • Enhanced Offline OData Progress Feedback

Contact Cell control enhancements

The ContactCell component now supports:

  • User Initials: displaying user initials, which is used when profile pictures are not available.
  • BadgeImage: this new property allows you to attach an additional indicator icon or image to the existing DetailImage or DetailImageText for each contact. For example, it can be used to highlight and identify primary contacts in a contact list.

Figure 8: Contact Cell control enhancements. Alt Text: iPhone and Android phone screens showing list of contacts with indicator icon with initials for each.

Find out more here:

  • Contact Cell control enhancements

AI Notice Form Cell Control

As part of ongoing enhancements in embedded AI capabilities, a new FormCell control, AINoticeFormCell, is introduced to display an inline notice for AI-generated content that may require review before use. 

Key Benefits:

  • Clearly indicates when content is generated using AI.
  • Helps users understand that AI-generated content may need validation.
  • Supports optional links for additional context or guidance.

Figure 9: AI notice form cell control. Alt Text: iPhone and Android phone screens showing various short and long AI notice messages such as “This result was produced by an AI model. Verify before use.”

Find out more here:

  • AI Notice Form Cell Control

AI Feedback Form Cell Control

As part of the embedded AI enhancement area, a new FormCell control, AIFeedback, is introduced to enable quick user feedback on AI-generated content. The control provides thumbs-up and thumbs-down options along with a caption and is designed specifically for AI-related experiences.

Figure 10: AI feedback form cell control. Alt Text: iPhone and Android phone screens showing various options for thumbs up and down feedback selectors.

Find out more here:

  • AI Feedback Form Cell Control

Stepper Form Cell Control

We have introduced a new FormCell control, Stepper, to allow users to increase or decrease numeric values using buttons or direct input. The control supports configurable step size, value range limits, decimal precision, and validation.

Key Benefits:

  • Enables easy adjustment of numeric values through stepper buttons or manual entry.
  • Supports configurable increments for flexible use cases.
  • Allows enforcement of minimum and maximum value limits.
  • Provides control over numeric precision for consistent input formatting.

Figure 11: Stepper Form Control. iPhone and Android phone screens showing three different stepper controls with + and – selectors and the value in between, with a popover showing “Alert: Stepper value is 4” and an OK button.

Find out more here:

  • Stepper Form Cell Control

Enhanced Offline OData Progress Indicator For Long-Running Tasks

Offline OData operations now provide step-level progress messages, offering improved visibility into long-running tasks such as initialization, download, upload, and send store. Localized default messages are displayed automatically with no additional configuration.

Key Benefits:

  • Introduces step-level progress updates for offline operations.
  • Improves visibility into long-running processes such as sync and data transfer.
  • Provides localized default messages out of the box.
  • Enables customization and runtime control of progress feedback.
  • Progress messages can be customized using the ProgressMessages property under OfflineOptions in the .service definition. These messages are used during offline operations including initialization, download, upload, and send store.

Figure 12: Offline progress indicator. Animated video of iPad and Android phone screens showing progress over time of a 20 step process, with the current step counter being incremented along with a text for each step.

Find out more here:

  • Enhanced Offline OData Progress Feedback.

Further MDK updates

I picked the above highlights, but there are quite a few more enhancements in the last two MDK releases. To get the full overview, have a look at these two blog posts:

  • What’s new in Mobile development kit client 26.6

entry.title: Deploying SAPUI5 Apps to SAP Build Work Zone
entry.content:
Introduction

While working with SAPUI5 applications, I wanted to understand how an application developed in SAP Business Application Studio could be made available to users through SAP Build Work Zone. Creating and running the application locally was straightforward, but the deployment and Work Zone configuration involved a few additional steps.

I went through the complete process of creating a simple SAPUI5 application, configuring it for deployment to Cloud Foundry, and then making the deployed application available in SAP Build Work Zone. One thing I found useful was understanding how the application moves from BAS to Cloud Foundry and then becomes available through Work Zone's Content Explorer.

During the setup, I also noticed that successfully deploying the application to Cloud Foundry was only one part of the process. Work Zone needed to be refreshed before the deployed HTML5 application became available for import. This was one of the practical details that helped me understand how the different parts of the setup are connected.

In this blog, I'll walk through the approach step by step. By the end, you'll have a SAPUI5 application deployed to Cloud Foundry and available as a tile inside a SAP Build Work Zone site.

Step 1: Subscribe to SAP Build Work Zone

First, we need access to SAP Build Work Zone.

Open the SAP BTP Cockpit and navigate to:

Service Marketplace → SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition → Standard Subscription

Subscribe to the service.

This screenshot shows the SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition subscription option in the SAP BTP Service Marketplace.

The subscription gives us access to the Work Zone capabilities that we will use later to create a site and make our deployed application available to users.

Step 2: Assign the Launchpad Admin Role

After subscribing, we need the required permissions to manage Work Zone.

Go to:

Security → Users

Select your user and choose:

Assign Role Collection → Launchpad_Admin

Assign the role collection to your user.

After assigning the role, log out and log in again so that the updated permissions are applied.

This screenshot shows the Launchpad_Admin role collection being assigned to the user.

One small thing I noticed during the setup was that assigning the Launchpad_Admin role collection did not immediately reflect in my current session. I had to log out and log in again before the updated permissions were available.

This was useful to know because, without refreshing the session, it can look like the role assignment has not been applied correctly.

Step 3: Create a Site

Now open SAP Build Work Zone and go to:

Site Directory → Create Site

Give the site a suitable name and create it.

This screenshot shows the Site Directory where a new Work Zone site is created. The site will later contain the tile for our deployed SAPUI5 application.

At this point, we have the basic Work Zone setup ready. Next, we can create the SAPUI5 application that we want to deploy.

Step 4: Create a SAPUI5 Project

Now let's create the application that will eventually be deployed to Work Zone.

Open SAP Business Application Studio (BAS) and create a new project using:

New Project from Template → SAP Fiori Application → Basic App

For this example, I used a basic SAPUI5 application. The application is only used to demonstrate the deployment and Work Zone integration, but the same process can be followed for a real SAPUI5 or Fiori application.

Step 5: Enable Deployment Configuration

While creating the application, enable the deployment-related options:

  • Add deployment configuration
  • Add FLP configuration

These configurations are important because we are not only going to run the application locally. We also need the project to contain the configuration required for deployment and launchpad integration.

At this stage, BAS will add the required deployment and FLP-related configuration to the project.

Step 6: Select Cloud Foundry as the Deployment Target

For the deployment target, select:

Cloud Foundry

The application will be packaged and deployed to the Cloud Foundry environment in SAP BTP.

Make sure you have access to the required Cloud Foundry organization and space before starting the deployment.

Step 7: Configure the FLP Settings

Next, configure the launchpad-related information.

Provide values for:

  • Semantic Object
  • Action
  • Tile Title

For example:

Semantic Object: Employee
Action: display
Tile Title: Employee Application

These values are used when the application is exposed through the launchpad environment.

The exact values can be different depending on your application and navigation requirements.

Step 8: Run the Application Locally

Before deploying the application, I recommend checking that everything works locally.

Use the Preview Application option in BAS and verify that the application opens correctly.

For this example, you should see the basic application output, such as the Hello World screen.

This is a useful checkpoint because it allows us to make sure the application itself is working before moving on to the deployment steps.

Step 9: Build the MTA Project

Once the application is working, we need to create the deployment package.

In BAS, right-click:

mta.yaml → Build MTA Project

This generates the MTAR file that will be used for deployment to Cloud Foundry.

This screenshot shows the MTA project being built from mta.yaml. The generated MTAR package will be used for the Cloud Foundry deployment.

Step 10: Deploy to Cloud Foundry

After building the MTAR, deploy it to Cloud Foundry.

Start the deployment and log in when prompted.

During the deployment, make sure you select the correct:

  • Cloud Foundry Organization
  • Space

The MTAR package will then be deployed to the selected Cloud Foundry environment.

This screenshot shows the SAPUI5 application being deployed to the selected Cloud Foundry environment.

After deployment, I verified that the application was available under HTML5 Applications before moving on to the Work Zone configuration. This gave me a useful checkpoint to confirm that the Cloud Foundry deployment was completed successfully.

Step 11: Verify the Deployment

After the deployment is completed, open the SAP BTP Cockpit and check the HTML5 Applications section.

You should be able to find the deployed SAPUI5 application there.

This is an important checkpoint because it confirms that the application has been successfully deployed before we start configuring it in Work Zone.

Step 12: Refresh the HTML5 Applications in Work Zone

Now go back to SAP Build Work Zone.

Open:

Channel Manager

and refresh the HTML5 applications.

This allows Work Zone to detect the application that was recently deployed to Cloud Foundry.

This screenshot shows the Channel Manager being refreshed so that the newly deployed HTML5 application becomes available in Work Zone.

One thing that became clear to me during the process was that deploying the application to Cloud Foundry is not enough for it to immediately appear in Work Zone's Content Explorer.

This was the step that initially made the relationship between Cloud Foundry and Work Zone clearer to me.

After the deployment, I had to go to Channel Manager and refresh the HTML5 Applications content. Only after Work Zone refreshed the available applications could I continue to Content Explorer and add the deployed application.

This helped me understand the separation between the Cloud Foundry deployment and the Work Zone content configuration. The application can be successfully deployed, but Work Zone still needs to detect that newly deployed application before it can be added to the site.

Step 13: Import the Application

Next, go to:

Content Manager → Content Explorer → HTML5 Apps

Find your application and select Add.

This imports the deployed application into the Work Zone content environment.

This screenshot shows the deployed application available under HTML5 Apps in Content Explorer. The application is selected to add it to the Work Zone content.

At this point, I could see the application that had been deployed earlier in BAS and Cloud Foundry. This helped confirm that the application had successfully moved from the deployment environment into the Work Zone content environment.

Step 14: Create a Group

Now create a group for the application.

Go to:

Content Manager → Create → Group

Enable the Assignment Status option and save the group.

For example:

Group Name:
My Applications

This screenshot shows the creation of a Work Zone group that will be used to organize the application content.

Step 15: Assign the Application to the Everyone Role

Next, open:

Content Manager → Everyone Role

Assign the application to this role and save the changes.

This screenshot shows the SAPUI5 application being assigned to the Everyone role so that it can be made available to users accessing the site.

One thing I learned here was that importing an application into Work Zone is not the same as making it available to users. The application also needs to be assigned to the appropriate role and included in the site's content. This was an important distinction for me when I was going through the setup for the first time.

Step 16: Verify the Application in the Site

Finally, open the Work Zone site that you created earlier.

You should now see the application tile.

Click the tile and verify that the SAPUI5 application opens correctly.

This screenshot shows the SAPUI5 application displayed as a tile in the SAP Build Work Zone site. Selecting the tile launches the deployed application.

Key Learnings

During this implementation, a few things became clearer to me:

1. Role changes may require a new session

After assigning the Launchpad_Admin role collection, logging out and logging in again ensured that the updated permissions were available.

2. Cloud Foundry deployment and Work Zone configuration are separate steps

A successful Cloud Foundry deployment does not automatically mean that the application is immediately available in the Work Zone content environment. Checking the HTML5 Applications section first provides a useful checkpoint.

3. Refreshing Channel Manager is an important step

After deploying the application, refreshing the HTML5 Applications in Channel Manager allowed Work Zone to detect the newly deployed application. This helped me understand why an application that is already deployed may not immediately appear in Content Explorer.

Conclusion

When I first worked through this setup, the process looked like several independent configuration steps. After completing it, the overall flow became much clearer to me.

The most useful thing I learned was that deploying a SAPUI5 application to Cloud Foundry is only one part of making it available through SAP Build Work Zone. The application still needs to be detected by Work Zone, imported through Content Explorer, assigned to the appropriate role, and made available through a site.

Two small details were particularly useful during my setup: logging in again after assigning the Launchpad_Admin role collection and refreshing the HTML5 applications in Channel Manager after deployment. These helped me understand why newly assigned permissions or newly deployed applications may not be immediately reflected in the existing Work Zone session.

The overall flow became clear to me as:

BAS → Cloud Foundry → HTML5 Applications → Channel Manager → Content Explorer → Role/Group → Work Zone Site

Once this flow is understood, the same approach can be applied to other SAPUI5 applications that need to be made available through SAP Build Work Zone.

entry.title: Software 3.0 - AI & Agentic Engineering for SAP Fiori and SAPUI5 Development
entry.content:
Agentic AI can now produce a working SAPUI5 application in hours rather than weeks.

The engineering question is no longer whether an agent can write the code, but how a Fiori development team keeps that speed inside enterprise design, data and release discipline. 

 A recent SAP Community article, “How to use the new Google IDE Antigravity with SAP (and CAP)”, provides a useful prelude to this discussion. It shows how an agent-first development environment can be connected to the SAP ecosystem: install Node.js and the development kit, configure SAP extensions, and expose project context through an MCP server. 

The toolchain used throughout this walkthrough: SAPUI5 in Google AntiGravity. 

But installing an agentic IDE is only the beginning. The more important question is this: what does it mean, to engineer a production-grade SAP Fiori application when agents such as Claude and Gemini can already generate a full SAPUI5 application that follows SAP Fiori design guidelines and best practices? These agents no longer stop at generation. They inspect the repository, edit several files at once, run the application against mock data, observe failures and revise their own work.

The definition of development work is changing. 

This article sets out a step-by-step path for using agentic coding to build SAPUI5 applications. The method is not theoretical — it has produced thousands of lines of code across several SAPUI5 Fiori applications, running in production. Each step is illustrated with numbered screenshots from that work, so the method can be verified. 

By the end of this article you will be able to scaffold a SAPUI5 project with SAP Fiori tools, brief an agent against the SAP Fiori Design Guidelines, validate the screen with mock data, map every binding to OData metadata, prove the application under realistic system load, and release it through a governed transport.

 

Software 3.0 changes the Fiori software development lifecycle at its core.

In the agentic era, the Fiori expert defines the experience and the guardrails, uses SAP Fiori tools to establish the project correctly, and treats an AI agent such as Google Antigravity or Claude Code as an implementation partner that can plan, edit, run, inspect and refine the application. This article follows that workflow in Google Antigravity, which Google describes as an “agent-first development platform” where agents plan, execute and verify complex work across the editor, terminal and browser, and where tangible artifacts such as implementation plans, browser controls and screenshots make the work easy for a human to verify.

The Core idea is to have production-ready SAPUI5 Fiori application, moving through six controlled stages: scaffold, prompt, simulate, map, load-test, and release.

The working model is simple. Start with SAP Fiori Guided Development, let the agent generate and refine the UI, and validate it with mock data. Map every binding against the OData metadata and the underlying Virtual Data Model (VDM), the CDS-based model that an S/4HANA service exposes. Then prove the application under realistic system load before moving it to production.

This makes Software 3.0 tangible for Fiori: the human defines the business outcome, architecture and guardrails, while the agent performs the fast paced implementation, testing, debugging and iteration.

 

A. From Software 1.0 to Software 3.0

A useful way to think about the evolution is to ask how the developer programs in today's era. 

 

Era

Primary programming mechanism

Developer focus

Software 1.0

Hand-written code

Statements, functions, algorithms

Software 2.0

Auto-complete, Code generation, Pair Programming

Data, objective, logic.

Software 3.0 (Since early 2026 onwards)

Natural-language instructions + AI agents

Context, architecture, constraints, verification

 

New Development Plan: Requirement -> Architect -> Agent Plan -> Multi-file Implementation -> Diff Checks -> Runtime Verification -> Agentic PRs/ Release

The result is a different development loop. Instead of write, run, debug and repeat, the cycle becomes state the intent, review the agent's plan, let it implement across files, then check diffs and the runtime evidence it returns. The developer's time moves from typing the change to judging whether the change is right.

 

B. The Six-Step Agentic Fiori Method

The Agentic UI5 development model deliberately separates Fiori element design, frontend implementation, system testing, and production governance. That separation is what prevents a fast prototype from becoming an ungoverned production change.

 

Stage

Human owns

Agent accelerates

Evidence before moving on

1. Create the foundation

App scope, Fiori floorplan, service target

Project files, manifests, initial views

A runnable Freestyle project with a clear file structure

2. Prompt the UI5 implementation

Fiori Design Guidelines, responsive behaviour, naming rules

Multi-file XML/JS/i18n/CSS changes and refactoring, logic builds

Diff review, design checklist, and a working local preview

3. Test with mock data

Scenarios, edge cases, expected states

Mock data generation, loading states, error cases

Repeatable local tests with metadata-accurate responses

4. Map XML OData metadata

VDM/service semantics, key fields, associations, business rules

Entity-to-control mapping and binding scaffolding

A mapping table, validated bindings

5. Move into SAP Business Application Studio for full-system testing

Test scope, destinations, authorizations, performance thresholds

Test harnesses, scripts, diagnostics, and remediation proposals

System-level test results and resolved defects

6. Implement in production

Approval, security, transport, rollout, support

Build checks, release notes, deployment assistance

Approved artifact deployed to Production via the Transport and App visible through the intended launchpad path

 

 

C. Walkthrough: the six steps in practice

Before working through the six steps, lets put the baseline in place. You need Node.js with the UI5 tooling; SAP Fiori tools (Application Wizard, Guided Development and Service Modeler) in Visual Studio Code or SAP Business Application Studio; an agentic IDE such as Google Antigravity; a development OData service, or a saved copy of its $metadata document; and a destination or transport path to the target system. Every step below assumes this baseline exists. 

Figure 1. SAP UI5  tools in NPM package

 

1. Create a Freestyle Fiori application with Fiori Guided Development

Start with the SAP-aware foundation instead of asking an agent to invent a UI5 project structure. SAP Fiori tools in Visual Studio Code gives you three things you need in sequence: an Application Wizard that generates both SAP Fiori elements and freestyle SAPUI5 templates, Guided Development that applies supported how-to guidance for adding functionality, and a Service Modeler that lets you inspect the OData metadata behind the service, including entities, properties and associations. This matters because the wizard produces the layout, manifest and build configuration that SAP itself supports, so the agent works inside a structure the platform can run, test and deploy.

The accurate working pattern is therefore: use the Application Wizard to create the Freestyle SAPUI5 project, then use Guided Development and the Fiori Tools modelers to establish supported patterns.

The initial project should contain a predictable structure: manifest.json, Component.js, XML views, controllers, fragments, i18n resources, models, test folders, and a localService area for mock assets.

2. Prompt the UI5 implementation against SAP Fiori Design Guidelines

Open the generated codebase in the agentic IDE ie Google Antigravity. Now-forth, we will use Natural language for Prompting and will bring  the required features to existence. The quality of an agentic result depends on the quality of the context you give it. Do not prompt with “build me a dashboard.” Give Antigravity a structured brief: the business task and the persona it serves,  the entity sets and fields to bind, the files it may touch, the conventions it must obey, and the checks that must pass before it reports back.

This is where SAP Fiori expertise matters most. The agent should be instructed to preserve responsive behavior, clear information hierarchy, meaningful empty and busy states, content density, internationalization and semantic status colors. It should also understand that XML views, controllers, formatters, manifest.json, and i18n.properties form one coordinated change rather than six unrelated files. This is where the "TASTE" of the developer/Functional Profession matters in designing the UX.
