entry.title: Sending Emails from SAP CAP Applications Using Microsoft 365 & Microsoft Graph API
entry.content:
In this blog, we will learn how to send emails from an SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) application using Microsoft Graph API.

Instead of storing Microsoft credentials directly in the CAP application, we will configure the OAuth credentials in an SAP BTP Destination and let the SAP Cloud SDK use that destination when calling Microsoft Graph.

The complete flow looks like this:

The CAP application will expose a simple action:

We can then call this action from Postman, another application, or another backend process.

Prerequisites

Before starting, make sure you have:

  • Microsoft work account
  • Microsoft 365 / Exchange Online mailbox
  • Permission to create an App Registration
  • Permission to grant admin consent for API permissions
  • SAP BTP account
  • SAP CAP Node.js application

Security note: Never publish your actual Client Secret, Tenant ID, or other sensitive credentials in a GitHub repository or SAP Community article.

Part A – Configure Microsoft Entra ID

Step 1 – Open Microsoft Azure Portal

Open the Microsoft Azure Portal and sign in using your Microsoft work or school account.

Search for and open:

Microsoft Entra ID

Step 2 – Get the Tenant ID

Inside Microsoft Entra ID, open the tenant overview.

You will find the Tenant ID.

Copy this value and keep it safely because we will use it later when configuring the SAP BTP Destination.

What is Tenant ID?

The Tenant ID identifies your Microsoft Entra organization.

Step 3 – Register an Application

Navigate to: Microsoft Entra ID → App registrations

Select: New registration

For this example, we will use:

Application name: SAP-CAP-Mail-Sender

Supported account types

Microsoft provides different options when registering an application.

The available options include scenarios such as:

  • Accounts in this organizational directory only
  • Accounts in any organizational directory
  • Accounts in any organizational directory and personal Microsoft accounts
  • Personal Microsoft accounts only

For this implementation, select:

Accounts in this organizational directory only

Why do we choose Single Tenant?

Our CAP application is intended to communicate with a mailbox belonging to one Microsoft 365 organization.

We therefore don't need users from other Microsoft Entra tenants to authenticate with this application.

A single-tenant application keeps the application scoped to the organization's own Microsoft Entra directory.

For a multi-tenant SaaS application, the design would be different and a multi-tenant registration could be considered.

For this use case, select the single-tenant option and click Register.

For Redirect URI, we don't need to configure one for this server-to-server client-credentials scenario.

Step 4 – Collect Application Information

After registration, open:

SAP-CAP-Mail-Sender → Overview

You will find:

  • Application (client) ID
  • Directory (tenant) ID

Copy both values.

Your configuration notes should now look like:

Microsoft Graph Configuration

=============================

Application Name: SAP-CAP-Mail-Sender

Client ID: <your-client-id>

Tenant ID:<your-tenant-id>

Step 5 – Create a Client Secret

Navigate to: Certificates & secrets

Under Client secrets, select: New client secret

Provide a description such as:  SAP CAP Mail Integration

Select an expiration period according to your organization's policy.

Click Add.

Microsoft will display information including:

  • Description
  • Secret ID
  • Value
  • Expiration

Important

Copy the Value immediately.

The secret value is only displayed when the secret is initially created.

The Secret ID is not the value that the application uses for authentication.

Your configuration notes should now look like:

Microsoft Graph Configuration

=============================

Client ID: <your-client-id>

Tenant ID: <your-tenant-id>

Client Secret: <your-client-secret>

Security

Do not place the client secret in:

  • GitHub
  • CAP source code
  • Frontend JavaScript
  • package.json
  • Public configuration files

For this architecture, the credentials will be maintained in the SAP BTP Destination.

Step 6 – Configure Microsoft Graph API Permissions

Now open: API permissions → Add a permission

Select: Microsoft Graph

Then select:  Application permissions

Why Application Permissions?

Our CAP backend needs to send an email without requiring a user to be interactively logged in.

The flow is:

There is no browser-based user authentication involved when the CAP backend calls Graph using the client-credentials approach.

Therefore, we use Application permissions for this app-only scenario.

Step 7 – Add Mail.Send Permission

Under Application permissions, search for: Mail.Send

Expand: Mail

Select: Mail.Send

Then click: Add permissions

The permission allows the registered application to send email using Microsoft Graph.

Step 8 – Grant Admin Consent

Application permissions require administrator consent.

If you have the required administrator privileges, grant consent for the organization.

After consent has been successfully granted, the permission should show as granted for the tenant.

Without the required consent, the CAP application will not be able to obtain the required application access to Microsoft Graph.

Important Security Consideration

At this point, the application has the:

Mail.Send

application permission.

Depending on the organization's Microsoft 365 configuration, this can provide broad mail-sending capability.

For a production implementation, the Microsoft 365 administrator should consider restricting the application to only the mailbox or mailboxes that the application actually needs.

This is especially important when using application permissions because the application is not acting on behalf of an individual interactive user.

At this point, Your configuration notes should now look like:

Microsoft Graph Configuration
=============================
Application Name: SAP-CAP-Mail-Sender
Tenant ID: <YOUR_TENANT_ID>
Client ID: <YOUR_CLIENT_ID>
Client Secret: <YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET>
Sender Email: <YOUR_MAILBOX>
Graph Permission: Mail.Send
Admin Consent: Granted

Step 9 – Identify the Sender Mailbox

We now need a Microsoft 365 mailbox from which the application will send emails.

For example: sender@yourcompany.com

The mailbox will later be referenced in the Microsoft Graph endpoint:

/v1.0/users/<sender-mailbox>/sendMail

Microsoft Configuration Completed

At this point, Your configuration notes should now look like:

Microsoft Graph Configuration
=============================
Application Name: SAP-CAP-Mail-Sender
Tenant ID: <YOUR_TENANT_ID>
Client ID: <YOUR_CLIENT_ID>
Client Secret: <YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET>
Sender Email: <YOUR_MAILBOX>
Graph Permission: Mail.Send
Admin Consent: Granted

Part B – Configure SAP BTP Destination

Now that Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft Graph are configured, we can connect the SAP CAP application to Microsoft Graph through an SAP BTP Destination.

Navigate to:

SAP BTP Cockpit → Connectivity → Destinations

Create a new destination.

Use the following configuration pattern:

Name: MS_GRAPH_MAIL

Type: HTTP

URL: https://graph.microsoft.com

Proxy Type: Internet

Authentication:OAuth2ClientCredentials

Configure the OAuth credentials: Client ID(<YOUR_CLIENT_ID> )

Client Secret:<YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET>

For the token service URL, use:

https://login.microsoftonline.com/<TENANT_ID>/oauth2/v2.0/token

Add the OAuth scope: https://graph.microsoft.com/.default

The .default scope tells Microsoft Entra ID to issue a token containing the application permissions that have already been configured and consented for the application.

After completing the configuration, the destination should contain the required connectivity and authentication information.

 

Why use a BTP Destination?

Instead of writing credentials directly inside the CAP application, the application only refers to:

destinationName: "MS_GRAPH_MAIL"

The SAP Cloud SDK resolves the destination and uses the configured authentication details when making the request.

This keeps authentication configuration outside the application source code and makes it easier to manage between environments.

Part C – Create the CAP Mail Service

Now let's expose an action from our CAP service that accepts:

  • Recipient
  • Subject
  • Body

For example:

action sendMail(     to: String,     subject: String,    body: String ) returns String;

 

This allows another application or API client to call the CAP service and request an email to be sent.

Step 10 – Install SAP Cloud SDK HTTP Client

From the CAP project directory, install:

npm install @SAP-cloud-sdk/http-client

We will use the HTTP client to execute the request through the BTP Destination.

Step 11 – Implement the CAP Action

The implementation performs the following operations:

  1. Read the action parameters.
  2. Validate the recipient, subject, and body.
  3. Identify the sender mailbox.
  4. Build the Microsoft Graph sendMail endpoint.
  5. Create the Microsoft Graph mail payload.
  6. Call Microsoft Graph through the BTP Destination.
  7. Return the result to the caller.
this.on("sendMail", async (req) => {

    try {
        const { to, subject, body } = req.data;

        // 1. Validate input
        if (!to) {
            return req.error(400, "Recipient email is required");
        }

        if (!subject) {
            return req.error(400, "Email subject is required");
        }

        if (!body) {
            return req.error(400, "Email body is required");
        }

        // 2. Sender mailbox
        const senderEmail = "your-sender@yourcompany.com";

        // 3. Microsoft Graph API URL
        const graphUrl =  `/v1.0/users/${encodeURIComponent(senderEmail)}/sendMail`;

        // 4. Microsoft Graph request body
        const mailPayload = {
            message: {
                subject: subject,
                body: {
                    contentType: "HTML",
                    content: body
                },
                toRecipients: [
                    {
                        emailAddress: {
                            address: to
                        }
                    }
                ]
            },
            saveToSentItems: true
        };

        // 5. Call Microsoft Graph through BTP Destination
        const response = await executeHttpRequest(
            {
                destinationName: "MS_GRAPH_MAIL"
            },
            {
                method: "POST",
                url: graphUrl,
                headers: {
                    "Content-Type": "application/json"
                },
                data: mailPayload
            }
        );

        // 6. Successful response
        console.log("Microsoft Graph response:", response.status);
        return "Email sent successfully";
    } catch (error) {
        console.error("Microsoft Graph email error:",    error.response?.data || error.message   );

        return req.error(
            500,
            "Failed to send email: " +
            (error.response?.data?.error?.message ||
             error.message)
        );
    }
});

Understanding the Important Part

The most important part of the implementation is:

const response = await executeHttpRequest(
    {
        destinationName: "MS_GRAPH_MAIL"
    },
    {
        method: "POST",
        url: graphUrl,
        headers: {
            "Content-Type": "application/json"
        },
        data: mailPayload
    }
);

The CAP application does not directly contain the OAuth token-generation logic.

This separation makes the application code simpler and keeps the authentication configuration in the BTP environment.

Step 12 – Configure the Sender Email

In the implementation:

const senderEmail = "your-sender@yourcompany.com";

Replace this with the Microsoft 365 mailbox that the application is configured to use.

The mailbox becomes part of the Microsoft Graph endpoint:

/v1.0/users/sender@example.com/sendMail

Step 13 – Bind the Destination for Local Testing

When running the CAP application locally, the application still needs access to the destination configuration.

Therefore, the corresponding destination service instance should be bound to the local CAP application/environment according to your BTP setup.

Once the destination is available to the local CAP application, we can test the service.

Step 14 – Test the CAP Service

Example request:

POST {{server}}/odata/v4/complaint/sendMail
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "to": "recipient@example.com",
    "subject": "Test from SAP CAP",
    "body": "<h2>Hello!</h2><p>This email was sent from SAP CAP using Microsoft Graph.</p>"
}

If the configuration is correct, the CAP service returns:

Email sent successfully

The recipient should then receive the email in their mailbox.

Understanding the Complete Flow

Let's look at what happens when we send the request.

 

Conclusion

In this implementation, we successfully integrated an SAP CAP application with Microsoft 365 email using Microsoft Graph API.

The important pieces are:

  • Microsoft Entra App Registration provides the application identity.
  • Mail.Send Application permission allows app-only mail sending.
  • Admin consent enables the configured application permission.
  • SAP BTP Destination stores the OAuth connectivity configuration.
  • SAP Cloud SDK resolves the destination from the CAP application.
  • The CAP service builds and sends the Microsoft Graph sendMail request.
  • The Microsoft 365 mailbox sends the final email.

The key advantage of this approach is that the CAP application does not need to manage Microsoft OAuth credentials directly in its source code. The authentication and connectivity configuration is maintained through the SAP BTP Destination while the application focuses on the business logic of sending the email.

entry.title: SAP Joule for Developers: End of the Promotional Period and The Path Forward
entry.content:
SAP Joule for Developers, which brought generative AI capabilities into SAP Build and ABAP at no additional cost during its initial promotional period, is ending on September 30th, 2026.  We are extending the promo offer for SAP Build features to December 31st, 2026, and this post explains exactly what that means for you, what happens to each capability you may be using today, and what your path forward looks like after December 31st, 2026. 

We know changes like this require planning, and we want to give you as much clarity as possible, well in advance, so you can make informed decisions for your team and your projects. 

What Does This Mean for You? 

If you are using SAP Build generative AI capabilities today — SAP Build Process Automation generative AI features or Joule Studio, classic edition generative AI features — you retain full access through December 31, 2026. AI chat in SAP Build Code is already rolled out in Business Application Studio and will continue beyond December 31, 2026. SAP Joule for Developers, ABAP AI capabilities will be commercially available starting October 1, 2026, outside the promotion (previously announced here). 

SAP Build continues as a customer-managed solution development platform for extending SAP applications. What is changing is the commercial structure behind certain AI capabilities that were offered on a promotional basis, and the transition of the SAP Joule for Developers brand that will only be associated with ABAP AI capabilities as we move into 2027. 

Why Are We Making This Change? 

SAP Joule for Developers promotional period was designed to give customers hands-on experience with generative AI in SAP Build without an immediate commercial commitment. That exploration phase has provided real-world signals on what delivers value. Based on customer feedback, we made deliberate decisions for each capability.  Where usage and value are clear, we are moving capabilities into supported commercial models; where strategic alternatives exist to deliver better customer value, we are directing investment accordingly. 

What Happens to Each Capability?

ABAP AI — Continues under commercial licensing 

As announced in May 2026, ABAP AI moves to consumption-based pricing (PUPM model) effective October 1, 2026. If you are currently using ABAP AI under SAP Joule for Developers promotional access, SAP will contact you before the transition date with licensing details. More details available here. 

Action required: Plan for a licensing transition before October 1, 2026. 

AI assistance in SAP Build Code — Already Available in Business Application Studio 

AI Chat in SAP Build Code has already been rolled out in Business Application Studio (BAS) for those using build-code (SAP Build Code) or build-default (SAP Build Developer) plans. This will remain available beyond December 31, 2026. No action is required from customers; your AI coding assistance experience is uninterrupted and enhanced to now allow you to configure your own large language model provider, such as SAP AI Core, a third party LLM provider, or Github Copilot. 

SAP Build Process Automation GenAI features — Access through December 31, 2026 

SAP Build customers using generative AI features in SAP Build Process Automation — including process generation, decision generation, form generation, script generation, and summarization — can continue using those features until December 31, 2026. After December 31, 2026, you can continue using SAP Build Process Automation without generative AI support. You can begin exploring Joule Studio for a new agentic development experience once it is generally available in H2 2026. 

Your existing automations, processes, and decisions built in SAP Build Process Automation are unaffected. This transition impacts only the ability to use AI while authoring new content, not your existing artifacts.

Joule Studio, classic edition GenAI features — Access through December 31, 2026 

Customers using Joule Studio, classic edition can continue using its generative AI features such as agent creation and deletion, configuring agent properties, adding and removing tools, and triggering test modes until December 31, 2026. After December 31, 2026, you can continue using Joule Studio, classic edition, but without generative AI support. This specifically and only refers to the generative AI support during design time. You can begin exploring the new Joule Studio and its agentic development experience once it is generally available in H2 2026. 

Frequently Asked Questions 

Is SAP Build being deprecated? 

No. SAP Build continues as a customer managed application development platform for extending SAP applications, automations and digital workspaces. 

Do my existing SAP Build projects, automations, and code get affected? 

No. Your built artifacts are fully intact. Only AI-assisted authoring capabilities are affected by this transition. 

Can I keep using SAP Build Process Automation GenAI features and Joule Studio, classic edition GenAI features? 

Yes — GenAI features continue up to December 31, 2026. After this time, Joule Studio, classic edition GenAI features such as agent creation and deletion, configuring agent properties, adding and removing tools, and triggering test mode will be removed. SAP Build Process Automation GenAI features such as artifact (process, form, data type, decision) creation with natural language will be removed. These GenAI features refer specifically and only to the generative AI support during design time.

What happens after December 31, 2026 for SAP Build Process Automation GenAI and Joule Studio, classic edition GenAI? 

For SAP Build Process Automation and Joule Studio, classic edition, you can continue using these products without generative AI support after December 31, 2026. You can begin exploring Joule Studio for a new agentic development experience once it is generally available in H2 2026. 

What about the AI assistance in SAP Build Code? 

AI Chat is already rolled out in Business Application Studio (BAS) and continues beyond December 31, 2026. No action needed. 

Will ABAP AI Capabilities still be available after the promotional period ends? 

Yes — ABAP AI capabilities moves to the Per User Per Month (PUPM) commercial license from October 1, 2026. ABAP Development Tools remain free; only the AI capabilities require licensing. 

What should I do right now? 

If you use ABAP AI, engage your SAP account manager to plan the licensing transition before October 1, 2026. For SAP Build Process Automation GenAI and Joule Studio, classic edition, you can continue using SAP Build Process Automation and Joule Studio, classic edition without generative AI support after December 31st, 2026.  

You can begin exploring Joule Studio for a new agentic development experience once it is generally available in H2 2026. 

Who do I contact with questions? 

Your SAP account manager or Customer Success Partner. Or leave a comment below. 

 

Next Steps

  1. If you use SAP Joule for Developers, ABAP AI Capabilities — engage your SAP account manager now to plan the AI Units licensing transition before October 1, 2026. Purchase the AI Units contract (SKU 8019164) on the SAP Store. 
  2. If you use SAP Build Process Automation GenAI features or Joule Studio, classic edition genAI features, your access continues through December 31, 2026. After that date, you can continue using SAP Build Process Automation and Joule Studio, classic edition without generative AI support. You can begin exploring Joule Studio once it is generally available in H2 2026. 
  3. If you use the AI chat in SAP Build Code — no action needed. The capability continues in Business Application Studio beyond December 31, 2026 under fair use limits and is enhanced to now allow you to configure your own large language model provider, such as SAP AI Core, a third party LLM provider, or Github Copilot. 
  4. Share this post internally with developers, architects, and project owners who need to plan for these changes.

If you have questions, please leave a comment below or reach out to your SAP account manager or Customer Success Partner.

entry.title: What’s new in Mobile development kit client 26.9
entry.content:
Dear Community,

I'm happy to announce that a new release of the Mobile development kit (MDK) is now available for all SAP Build and Mobile Services customers. You can download it from the SAP Software Center, or from the community download page.

The SAP Mobile Services Client version 26.9.0 is available on Google Play and Apple App stores.

SAP MDK enables developers and technical business users to build cross-platform mobile applications. It allows you to build your application once, in an integrated development environment (Visual Studio Code / SAP Business Application Studio) and run it natively on Mobile (iOS & Android).  

The following enhancements are available only on iOS and Android platforms:

  • Supportability Enhancements
    • Support Crash Reporting
    UI Enhancements
    • Improved Sync Error Handling for Multi-User Switching
    • Display Attachment Title and File Size in Attachment Form Cell
    • Custom Search Icon Support for Text Input, List Picker, and Section Search 
    • Support Section page as Filter page
    MDK Editor Updates 
    • Automatic Dependencies Checks in MDK Editor VS Code Extension 
    • From MDK Genie to Agentic Development (Applicable in SAP Business Application Studio)

Support Crash Reporting

With this release, your MDK apps can now automatically capture and report crash data to SAP Mobile Services, giving administrators greater visibility into app stability issues in production. This enables teams to investigate crashes more efficiently.

Key Benefits

  • Faster troubleshooting: Crash logs are automatically uploaded to mobile services and provide valuable diagnostic information that can help developers and administrators investigate and resolve app crashes more efficiently.
  • User privacy and control: Crash data is uploaded only after the user has provided consent, with the consent decision stored per user and device.
  • Mobile Services controlled configuration: Administrators can enable or disable crash reporting through the mobile services admin UI without requiring changes to the app.
    Admin settings for crash log upload
  • In-app consent management:  App developers can expose crash reporting preferences in the app settings, allowing users to view or change their consent.
    Crash Report Collection Consent View
  • Improved app stability monitoring: Administrators can access crash information to better understand app stability and identify recurring issues.
    Uploaded Crash Logs page in mobile services admin UI

Client APIs: Three new client APIs allow apps to query and manage consent from within the app settings page.

  • isCrashReportingEnabled(): Returns true when crash reporting is enabled in the mobile services and app is not in demo mode.
let crashReportStatus = context.isCrashReportingEnabled();​
  • isCurrentCrashConsentAllowed(): Returns true if user has granted consent for crash reporting.
let consentAllowedStatus = context.isCurrentCrashConsentAllowed();​
  • showCrashConsentDialog(): Programmatically displays the crash reporting consent dialog. App developers should expose the crash consent screen in the app settings so users can review or change their preference. An error apperas if crash reporting is not enabled in the mobile services or when running in demo mode.
export default function CrashConsentDialog(context) {
    try {
        context.showCrashConsentDialog();
    } catch (error) {
        alert('Error showing crash consent dialog: ' + error.message);
    }
}​

For more information, refer to this documentation.

Improved Sync Error Handling for Multi-User Switching

We have improved sync error handling for multi-user scenarios, particularly when a previous user leaves unresolved business data on a shared device.
Previously, if a user made local changes, encountered a sync error, and logged off without resolving it, the next user could not continue using the app. On devices managed by MDM, where reinstalling the app may not be an option, this could leave the device unusable until the previous user returned to resolve the issue.
By default, when offline conflict handling is not configured, the only available action is Return to Sign In Screen. The previous user must sign in again and resolve the transaction issue before another user can continue using the app.
With MDK 26.9, configurable conflict handling allows the next user to resolve the previous user's pending transactions directly from the Transaction Issue screen and continue to the app without requiring the previous user to sign in again.

Key Benefits

  • Improved device availability: The next user can continue using the app even when the previous user is unavailable to resolve pending offline transactions.
  • Simplified user switching: Users can resolve or discard the previous user's pending transactions directly from the Transaction Issue screen without requiring the previous user to sign in again.
  • Administrator control: Administrators can enable offline conflict handling and select how pending transactions should be handled.
  • Data recovery option: When configured, a snapshot of the previous user's pending offline data can be uploaded before the transactions are discarded, providing an option for administrator recovery.

Configure Conflict Resolution in Mobile Services: To enable conflict resolution for multi-user mode:

  • In the Mobile Services cockpit, navigate to your application.
  • Under Shared Devices, enable Allow Upload of Pending Changes from Previous User.
  • Enable Offline Conflict Handling in Multi-User Mode.

    Admin settings to enable offline conflict handling

  • Select the desired conflict resolution mode:
    •  Discard Pending Transactions: Discards the previous user's pending transactions immediately.
    • Discard Pending Transactions After Upload: Uploads a snapshot of the previous user's offline data to the server for potential administrator recovery, and then discards the pending transactions. This requires:
      • Enable the offline store upload policy in mobile services
        Admin settings to enabel offline store upload
      • metadata changes using OfflineOptions.MultiUserConflictHandling in the .service file
//Excerpt of a .service file 
   "OfflineOptions": {
        "StoreParameters": {},
        "MultiUserConflictHandling": {
            "UploadEncryptionKey": "/MyApp/Rules/GenKey.js",
            "UploadRequestQueueOnly": true
        }
    },​

Runtime Behavior

When offline conflict handling is enabled, a conflict-handling action is displayed alongside Return to Sign In Screen on the Transaction Issue screen. When the user selects the conflict-handling action, a confirmation dialog is displayed before the selected action is applied. After the user confirms:

  • The configured conflict resolution policy is applied.
  • The app proceeds directly to the new user's main page without requiring the previous user to sign in.

If the user cancels the confirmation dialog or selects Return to Sign In Screen:

  • No conflict resolution is performed.
  • The previous user can sign in again and resolve the transaction issue manually.

 Runtime behavior on iOS and Android platforms


For more information, refer to this documentation.

Display Attachment Title and File Size in Attachment Form Cell

The MDK Attachment Form Cell now displays the attachment title (file name) and file size, making it easier for users to identify and review files before submission. This display is automatic and no metadata configuration changes are required.  Previously, users could not see the file name or size of an attachment, making it difficult to distinguish between files or understand their size.

Key Benefits

  • Improved file identification: Users can quickly distinguish between multiple attachments by their file name.
  • Better file awareness: Users can see the attachment size before submission or review.
  • Fiori UX alignment: The Attachment Form Cell experience is more consistent with standard Fiori UX expectations.

Examples displaying file name and size in FormCell attachment control

Custom Search Icon Support for Text Input, List Picker, and Section Search

MDK now supports custom icon configuration for TextInput (SimpleProperty), ListPicker, and Section controls, allowing app developers to replace default icons with custom images and provide a more tailored app experience.

All supported icon properties can reference metadata image paths, resource images, SAP icons, and font icons.

  • TextInput (SimpleProperty):  A new BarcodeIcon property allows developers to customize the barcode scanner button icon when AlternateInput is set to Barcode. A corresponding BarcodeIcon style class is available under Styles to customize the icon's color, font size, and background color.
//Excerpt of a page
{
    "BarcodeIcon": "sap-icon://action",
    "_Type": "Control.Type.FormCell.SimpleProperty",
    "_Name": "BarcodeSapIcon",
    "Caption": "Barcode Field sap-icon://",
    "PlaceHolder": "Scan here",
    "AlternateInput": "Barcode"
},

Search icon example in FormCell Simple Property

  • ListPicker and Section Search: New Icons and Styles properties are available under Search for both ListPicker and Section controls with Expandable or Persistent search.

//Excerpt of a page
{
    "_Type": "Control.Type.FormCell.ListPicker",
    "_Name": "ListPickerSapStyled",
    "AllowEmptySelection": true,
    "Caption": "sap-icon:// (Styled)",
    "IsEditable": true,
    "Search": {
        "Icons": {
            "Search": "sap-icon://show-edit",
            "Barcode": "/mdk269/Images/barcode.png",
            "Clear": "sap-icon://clear-all",
            "Styles": {
                "Search": "SearchAndSimplePropertyIconsStylesSmall",
                "Barcode": "SearchAndSimplePropertyIconsStylesSmall",
                "Clear": "SearchAndSimplePropertyIconsStylesSmall"
            }
        },
        "Placeholder": "Search items",
        "BarcodeScanner": true
    },
    "PickerItems": [
        "Apple",
        "Banana",
        "Cherry",
        "Date",
        "Elderberry"
    ]
},

"Search": {
    "Enabled": true,
    "Placeholder": "Search items",
    "BarcodeScanner": true,
    "Mode": "Persistent",
    "Icons": {
        "Search": "sap-icon://show-edit",
        "Back": "sap-icon://back-to-top",
        "Barcode": "sap-icon://qr-code",
        "Clear": "sap-icon://clear-all"
    }
},​

Support Section Page as Filter Page

 MDK now supports SectionedTable FormCellSection as a container for Filter pages, giving app developers a more structured and modern way to define filter controls while aligning with the latest recommended UI patterns.

Key Benefits:

  • Modern container structure: Use the consistent SectionedTable > FormCellSection > Form Cell Controls hierarchy, matching the rest of the application's page structure.
  • Future-proof implementation: FormCellContainer is soon to be deprecated; migrating to SectionedTable FormCellSection ensures long-term compatibility.
  • Unchanged filter logic: Target paths for accessing control values and the creation of filter criteria objects remain fully compatible — no changes needed to existing filter business logic.

Migration Notes:
When upgrading to MDK 26.9, you need to manually migrate existing filter pages from FormCellContainer to SectionedTable FormCellSection. The following changes are required:

  • Container definition structure: Update the page definition from FormCellContainer > Sections > Controls to SectionedTable > FormCellSection > Form Cell Controls.
  • Container retrieval rules: Update any rules that reference the container to reflect the new SectionedTable FormCellSection structure.
    Example of updating from FormCellContainer to SectionedTable
For more information, refer to this documentation.

Automatic Dependencies Checks in MDK Editor VS Code Extension

The MDK Editor extension now checks for all required prerequisites the moment it activates. If anything is missing, you're greeted with a Setup panel — not an error message.
MDK Editor Setup in VSC

The setup experience handles everything:

  • Missing VS Code extensions (Cloud Foundry Tools, Application Wizard) are installed with a single click using the VS Code Extensions API.
  • @SAP/generator-mdk is installed automatically via an integrated terminal task running npm install -g @SAP/generator-mdk.
  • CF CLI guidance is tailored to your operating system — no hunting for the right installer for Windows vs. macOS.
  • After installation, the extension re-validates your environment automatically.

A Clear Signal When You're Ready

Once all prerequisites are in place, the Setup panel gives you a full status summary: each prerequisite, its installed version, and whether updates are available. The "MDK Ready" checkmark in the VS Code status bar confirms your environment is good to go.

The MDK Editor Setup panel showing all prerequisites validated, with version details and update status at a glance. The "MDK Ready" indicator in the status bar confirms the environment is good to go.
MDK Editor Setup in Ready state

From MDK Genie to Agentic Development (Applicable in SAP Business Application Studio)

 MDK MCP Server is now accessible in SAP Business Application Studio via AI chat. The MDK MCP Server automatically plugs into your AI assistant and gives it real knowledge of the MDK metadata schema — not just generic code generation, but valid MDK artifacts it can reason about. That means:

  • Spin up a full MDK project from a prompt
  • Generate pages, actions, rules, i18n, services, styles — individually or together
  • Iterate on an existing project conversationally
  • Query MDK component schemas and client APIs inline via mdk-docs — no tab-switching, no docs hunting

Become an SAP MDK Explorer!
Do you have a requirement to build a mobile solution for your enterprise? Take your first steps today by following these tutorials to get started and learn more about the SAP Mobile development kit. We’re excited to see what you build—your feedback and ideas are invaluable!

Submit Improvement Requests
You can submit your improvement request here for Mobile development kit to the SAP Customer Influence site, a central place for all product improvement requests. You can browse all improvement requests, submit improvement requests, comment, vote, receive updates, and see who has voted at the SAP Customer Influence site.

entry.title: VSCode with S/4 Hana Classics (On Premise and Rise Private Edition) BTP Destinations
entry.content:
After many years of SAP projects, this is my first blog post here. The topic saves me time every day: running and deploying Fiori apps from my local VS Code against an on-premise S/4HANA system, through the same BTP destination and Cloud Connector that SAP Business Application Studio uses, without a dev space.

Update, October 2026: the first version of this post had you copy two scripts and edit YAML files by hand. A Yeoman generator now does all of that from the SAP Fiori tools Template Wizard, and it can set up several environments (dev, quality, production) in the same project. If you use Claude Code, a plugin does the same setup in a conversation; see "Set it up with Claude Code" below.

Why I stopped opening a dev space

SAP Business Application Studio is a good product, with generators, guided development and a toolchain ready in the browser. For many teams it is the right default. In daily work, though, I kept running into the same problems:

  • Disk space. Dev spaces have a limited quota, and a few node_modules folders plus an npm cache later I was cleaning up instead of developing.
  • Dev spaces that would not start, for no reason I could find. I waited, retried, and eventually created a new one.
  • npm run start hanging, again for no visible reason, while the same project and command worked fine locally.

So why open BAS at all? My laptop already has VS Code, Node.js, the Fiori tools and my extensions. The one thing it lacks is a route to the customer's S/4HANA: many customers only give access through remote desktops or VDIs, and the only path from outside into the backend is BTP and the Cloud Connector. What I need from BTP is the destination and the connectivity to the Cloud Connector.

I also tried the SAP Business Application Studio desktop client for VS Code. Underneath it is still a dev space, with the same disk quota and the same hanging npm start, plus containers that sometimes hang on start. I went the other way: keep everything local and borrow only the connectivity from BTP, through cf ssh port forwarding.

How it works

The connectivity proxy, which forwards HTTP calls into the Cloud Connector tunnel, can only be reached from the Cloud Foundry container network. Your laptop cannot reach it; any CF app container can.

A CF app bound to a destination and a connectivity service instance has all the credentials it needs in its environment (VCAP_SERVICES). If SSH is enabled for that app, cf ssh -L can forward a local port through the container to the connectivity proxy. A small Node.js proxy on your machine does the rest:

  1. The browser talks to fiori run on localhost as usual.
  2. fiori-tools-proxy sends /sap to the local proxy on port 5050 instead of to a destination.
  3. The local proxy adds what the connectivity proxy expects and sends the request into the cf ssh tunnel.
  4. Inside CF the request reaches the connectivity proxy, and the Cloud Connector calls the backend.

The CF app is only a jump host and its code never runs, so a 64 MB app that sleeps is enough. The wizard creates one if your space has none.

What happens at start-up

The proxy reads the app's bindings with cf app <app> --guid and cf curl /v3/apps/<guid>/env, using the CF session you already have. It keeps the destination and connectivity credentials in memory; it writes nothing to disk and creates no service key. It then gets one OAuth client-credentials token for the Destination service and one for the connectivity proxy, and refreshes each a minute before it expires.

Next it looks up the destination, which gives the virtual host URL, the sap-client and the CloudConnectorLocationId, and checks that the destination is of type OnPremise. Finally it opens cf ssh <app> -N -L 20003:<proxy host>:<proxy port>, with host and port taken from the connectivity binding, and starts listening on port 5050.

What happens on each request

The connectivity proxy is a plain HTTP forward proxy, so the outgoing request looks like one from a browser behind a corporate proxy: the request line carries the absolute URL of the destination's virtual host. The proxy adds Proxy-Authorization: Bearer <token> so the connectivity proxy knows the subaccount, and SAP-Connectivity-SCC-Location_ID when several Cloud Connectors are connected. It also adds the destination's sap-client when the request has none. For a destination with BasicAuthentication it sends the destination's logon. With NoAuthentication your own SAP logon passes through unchanged, so the backend still authenticates you, as it does in BAS.

The authentication problem I hit with fiori deploy

In our landscape the backend, reached through the Cloud Connector, only accepted a user and password after a first 401 round trip that sets the cookies sap-usercontext and sap-ssolist. Browsers and BAS do that round trip on their own. fiori deploy sends basic authentication straight away and ends with an authentication error, without a failed logon showing in SU01. That one cost me some time.

The proxy now handles it. When a request carries a basic logon but no sap-ssolist cookie, it first sends one anonymous request, collects the two cookies and adds them to the real request.

Prerequisites

In the BTP cockpit, a subaccount administrator needs to provide:

  • the entitlements Destination (plan lite), Connectivity (plan lite) and Cloud Foundry Runtime (64 MB of memory is enough);
  • a Cloud Connector connected to the subaccount that exposes the backend;
  • OnPremise destinations at subaccount level (Connectivity > Destinations). The local proxy has no user token, so only NoAuthentication and BasicAuthentication destinations work.

On your machine you need Node.js 22 or later and the cf CLI v8. Check with cf version. To install it, run winget install CloudFoundry.CLI.v8 (or choco install cloudfoundry-cli) on Windows, or brew install cloudfoundry/tap/cf-cli@8 on macOS, or use the installer from the official installation guide.

In the Cloud Foundry space you need the SpaceDeveloper role, which is required to read app environments and to use cf ssh, and SSH must be allowed for the space. If it is not, a Space Manager runs cf allow-space-ssh <space>.

Install the generator

npm install -g @scodigis/generator-btp-on-premise-scripts

Reopen the Template Wizard in VS Code (or in SAP Business Application Studio) and the BTP On-Premise Access tile appears. From a terminal you can also run yo @scodigis/btp-on-premise-scripts after npm i -g yo.

The source is on GitHub at https://github.com/DenisGalandSAP/generator-btp-on-premise-scripts, and the package is on npm at https://www.npmjs.com/package/@scodigis/generator-btp-on-premise-scripts.

The wizard, step by step

Project

Pick the folder of a SAPUI5 freestyle or SAP Fiori elements app and give the environment a name, such as dev. If you are already logged in to Cloud Foundry you can keep that session or log in to another region or subaccount; an environment that lives in another region needs a login there. If you are not logged in, the next step asks for the region and lets you log in with an SSO passcode or a user and password.

Cloud Foundry Target

Pick the org and space. When the space has exactly one app bound to both a destination and a connectivity instance, the wizard uses it. When it has none, the wizard offers to create btp-tunnel, a 64 MB app that only sleeps, and binds it to new or existing destination and connectivity instances. It also checks that SSH is enabled for the app.

Destinations

Pick the destination the running app uses and, if you also deploy through BTP, the deploy destination. They can be the same one or two different ones, for example one client for runtime and another for deployment. If you leave deployment unchecked, the wizard skips the next step.

Deployment

Enter the BSP application name, package, transport request and client. The wizard prefills them from an existing ui5-deploy.yaml. If the deploy destination has no authentication, it also asks for the ABAP user and password, which go into the environment's .env file. The generator adds that file to .gitignore.

What you get

For an environment called dev, the generator adds three scripts to a scripts/ folder, which only use Node.js built-ins. It also writes ui5-btp-dev.yaml, a copy of your ui5.yaml with the backend pointing at the local proxy, ui5-deploy-btp-dev.yaml for deployment, a .env.dev file with the settings, and a "Run with BTP destination (dev)" entry for F5 in VS Code. Your ui5.yaml and ui5-deploy.yaml stay as they are, so BAS keeps working for colleagues who prefer it.

CommandWhat it does
npm run start-btp:devStarts the app; every /sap call goes through the BTP destination and the Cloud Connector
npm run deploy-btp:devBuilds the app and deploys it to the ABAP repository through the deploy destination
npm run deploy-btp-test:devSame deployment in test mode, which writes nothing
npm run btp-proxy:devStarts only the proxy, for CAP, Postman or curl

Each command starts the tunnel and the proxy when needed and reuses them when they are already running for the same destination. Ctrl+C stops everything it started.

Several environments

Run the generator again with another name, say qual or prod, to add an environment. Each one keeps its own API endpoint, org, space, tunnel app, destinations, deploy target and credentials, so dev can sit in a subaccount in one region and prod in a subaccount in another.

Before starting a proxy, the scripts point the cf CLI at the environment. If only the org or space differs, they run cf target. If the region differs or the session has expired, they run cf login in the terminal. This changes your global cf target, so start environments that live in different regions one after the other: wait until the first proxy is up before starting the second. Environments in the same region can run side by side, because each gets its own ports.

Projects set up with the first version of this post, or with an earlier version of the generator, are migrated the first time you run the generator on them.

Set it up with Claude Code

If you work with Claude Code, you can skip the wizard. The plugin btp-on-premise-access asks the same questions in the chat and writes the same files. It runs the same code too: the npm package now has a command-line tool, btp-on-premise-setup, and the plugin calls it through npx.

Install it from Claude Code:

/plugin install btp-on-premise-access --marketplace DenisGalandSAP/generator-btp-on-premise-scripts

On Claude Code versions before 2.1.275, add the marketplace first:

/plugin marketplace add DenisGalandSAP/generator-btp-on-premise-scripts
/plugin install btp-on-premise-access@scodigis

Then open the app folder and ask something like "set up this app to run through our BTP destination for dev". You need Node.js 22 and the cf CLI, as for the generator, and nothing installed globally.

Here is a run on one of my apps, with the names changed. My cf session had expired, so Claude gave me the link to the passcode page. I pasted the one-time passcode, and it found the org, the space and the tunnel app on its own. It only asked where there was a real choice: the runtime destination, the deploy destination and the deploy target.

Claude checks the project, logs in with an SSO passcode and asks for the destinations.

Before writing anything, it shows a dry run with every file it will create or change. In my case it also pointed out that the transport belonged to another system than the one I deploy to. The wizard does not check that.

The dry run, with a warning about a transport from the wrong system.

After I said yes, it wrote the files and started npm run start-btp:dev. The first start failed because the project had no node_modules yet, so it ran npm install and started again, then waited until the proxy and the UI5 server were up.

Claude starts the app and waits for the proxy and the UI5 server.

The proxy runs through the tunnel app, and the app answers on localhost:8080.

Claude never asks for a password in the chat. A cf login with user and password happens in your own terminal, and you type the ABAP deploy password into .env.<env> yourself. The SSO passcode you paste works once and expires within minutes. The command-line tool also leaves destination passwords and client secrets out of everything it shows Claude.

Troubleshooting

SymptomFix
cf login starts when you run a scriptThe cf session expired, or the environment lives in another region. Log in and the command continues
No app in the space is bound to both servicesLet the wizard create btp-tunnel, or bind an existing app to a destination and a connectivity instance
SSH is disabled for the appcf enable-ssh <app> and cf restart <app>; if the space forbids SSH, a Space Manager runs cf allow-space-ssh <space>
Port 5050 or 20003 is used by another programClose that program or change the port in .env.<env>
403 "Access denied to resource … expose the resource in your cloud connector"That path is not exposed in the Cloud Connector; ask its administrators
Deploy ends with an authentication errorCheck USR / SAP_PWD in .env.<env>: it must be the password for the deploy client
Token request failed with 401The binding uses X.509 credentials; the proxy expects a client secret

Set BTP_PROXY_DEBUG=1 to log every request with its status and cookie names (never the values).

What about security?

Discuss this with your BTP administrators before you use it. My view:

  • It opens nothing new. Anyone who can cf ssh into an app and read its environment can do all of this by hand; the scripts need the same SpaceDeveloper rights and only automate those steps.
  • The BTP credentials and tokens live in memory for the lifetime of the proxy, with no service key and no file. The only secrets on disk are the ABAP deploy user and password, when you enter them, in a git-ignored .env.<env>.
  • The Cloud Connector stays in charge. Only the hosts and paths it exposes are reachable; everything else gets a 403, as it does from BAS.
  • The backend still authenticates you with your own SAP user when the destination has no authentication.
  • The proxy and the tunnel listen on 127.0.0.1 only, so other machines on your network cannot use them.
  • It is a development tool. Use it on development and test subaccounts, not as a production integration path.

Beyond Fiori: CAP and others

The proxy knows nothing about Fiori. It is an HTTP endpoint on 127.0.0.1:5050 that ends up in your backend. For a CAP project that consumes an on-premise OData service, start it with npm run btp-proxy:dev and point the remote service at it in a development profile:

"cds": {
  "requires": {
    "API_BUSINESS_PARTNER": {
      "kind": "odata-v2",
      "model": "srv/external/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER",
      "[development]": {
        "credentials": { "url": "http://127.0.0.1:5050/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER" }
      }
    }
  }
}

With BTP_PROXY_USER and BTP_PROXY_PWD set, cds watch talks to the real backend from your laptop. Postman, Bruno and curl work the same way.

Wrapping up

This setup removed a whole category of "why is it hanging today?" problems for me. My editor, Node version, disk and extensions are local and fast, and BTP provides the one thing my laptop cannot do alone: a trusted path through the Cloud Connector. I still use BAS when it makes sense, but when connectivity is the only reason to open it, cf ssh is enough.

This is my first post, so I would appreciate your feedback. Tell me whether it works in your landscape, which problems you hit, or whether you know a simpler way. See you in the comments.

entry.title: An End-to-End Travel Approval App with SAP CAP, HANA Cloud, and SAP Build Process Automation
entry.content:
Goal

The goal is to build a working Travel Approval application, not just a collection of disconnected demos. A user creates a travel request in a Fiori Elements application. The CAP service stores the request in SAP HANA Cloud and automatically starts an SAP Build Process Automation workflow.

The approver reviews the task in My Inbox and selects Approve or Reject, updating the corresponding Travel record in HANA Cloud.

Create Travel in Fiori
       ↓
CAP saves the active record in HANA Cloud
       ↓
CAP starts the BPA workflow automatically
       ↓
Approval task appears in SAP Build Lobby->My Inbox
       ↓
Approve → overall_status = A
Reject → overall_status = R
       ↓
Validate in Fiori, SAP Build->Monitoring, and HANA Database Explorer

Prerequisites

BTP Service / instance required
SAP Business Application Studio
SAP HANA Cloud
SAP Build Process Automation

The End-to-End Flow

  1. Create Travel entity in CDS.
  2. Expose the entity as a draft-enabled OData V4 service.
  3. Generate the Fiori Elements application.
  4. Bind the CAP project to the HANA HDI container.
  5. Build the MTA archive and deploy it to Cloud Foundry.
  6. Download the CAP metadata as an EDMX specification.
  7. Create SAP Build Actions from the EDMX and test the OData operations.
  8. Create the Travel Context, API trigger, Approval Form, and approval branches in BPA.
  9. Create a BPA service key and an API key with trigger execution permission.
  10. Add the CAP SAVE handler that starts the workflow automatically.
  11. Test from Fiori, process the task in My Inbox, monitor the instance in Build Lobby, and validate the final status in HANA.

1. Model the CDS Entity for the CAP OData V4 Service

The CDS entity is the source of truth for the Travel data. The technical UUID and the business Travel ID form the key used by the draft-enabled service and by the generated SAP Build Actions.

1.1.    Expose the Travel entity as a service

Create file srv/service.cds.

Why draft support matters: Fiori Elements creates and edits a draft first. The active Travel record is produced when the user activates or saves the draft. The CAP SAVE event is therefore the reliable point for starting the workflow.

2. Create the Fiori Elements App

Generate a List Report/Object Page application for CAPWFService.Travel. The list lets users create requests and review the current status. The Object Page captures the full Travel details.

 

Figure 1. Fiori List Report with Travel IDs in ascending order.

3. Connect to Cloud Foundry

3.1.    Cloud Foundry provides the runtime for the deployed CAP service. Log in from the BAS terminal and select the correct organization and dev space.

cf login
cf target

3.2.    Before testing SAP Build Actions, always confirm that the deployed CAP application is running:

cf start CAPWF-srv
cf app CAPWF-srv

3.3.    Expected status:

requested state: started
instances: 1/1
state: running

Important: When CAPWF-srv was stopped, every SAP Build Action returned 404 Requested route does not exist. Starting the application restored the Actions immediately.

4. Bind to a HANA Cloud HDI Container

An HDI container is an application-scoped database container. It gives the CAP application its own isolated schema inside the HANA Cloud database.

cds bind --to CAPWF-db
cds env get requires.db --profile hybrid

The hybrid profile must show the CAPWF-db instance. Start the local service against HANA:

pkill -f cds
cds watch --profile hybrid

Look for connect to db > hana and the expected HANA schema in the terminal output.

Lesson learned: The lowercase capwf-db and uppercase CAPWF-db were two separate service instances. Local Fiori and deployed BPA initially showed different record counts because they were connected to different HDI containers.

5. Generate the MTAR File

The Multi-Target Application archive packages the service, database deployer, security resources, destinations, and HTML5 content into one deployable unit.

mbt build

The archive is generated under: mta_archives/CAPWF_1.0.0.mtar

6. Deploy to HANA Cloud and Cloud Foundry

cf deploy mta_archives/CAPWF_1.0.0.mtar

The deployment runs the database deployer, binds CAPWF-srv to CAPWF-db and CAPWF-auth, and starts the application route.

cf app CAPWF-srv
cf routes
cf logs CAPWF-srv --recent

Free-tier note: Stopping applications frees runtime memory, but it also makes the CAP route unavailable. Start CAPWF-srv again before testing browser URLs or SAP Build Actions.

7. Connect to the HANA DB Explorer and Add the HDI Container

7.1.    Open SAP HANA Database Explorer.

7.2.    Choose Add Database or Add HDI Container.

7.3.    Select the CAPWF-db HDI container.

7.4.    Expand Catalog and Tables.

7.5.    Open the Travel table data and compare the record count with the Fiori app.

7.6.    After approval or rejection, refresh the table and verify overall_status.

Figure 2. CAPWF-db added to SAP HANA Database Explorer.

8. Download the Metadata File as EDMX

19. Start the Workflow Automatically from CAP

The Fiori application activates a draft when the user saves a new Travel. CAP handles that lifecycle through the SAVE event. The handler builds the exact trigger payload, obtains an OAuth token, sends the BPA API key, and creates the workflow instance.

// create a file in srv/service.js

this.after('SAVE', 'Travel', async (data, req) => {
   const travel = req.data;

   const workflowPayload = {
       definitionId:
         'us10.e66895ddtrial.rap110travelworkflow.travelApprovalProcessing',
       context: {
           travelContext: {
               TravelUUID: travel.ID,
               TravelID: travel.travel_id,
               IsActiveEntity: true,
               agency_id: travel.agency_id,
               customer_id: travel.customer_id,
               begin_date: travel.begin_date,
               end_date: travel.end_date,
               booking_fee: Number(travel.booking_fee),
               total_price: Number(travel.total_price),
               currency_code: travel.currency_code,
               description: travel.description,
               overall_status: travel.overall_status
           }
       }
   };

   // 1. Get an OAuth token with BPA client credentials.
   // 2. POST workflowPayload to BPA_WORKFLOW_URL.
   // 3. Send Authorization: Bearer <token> and api-key headers.
});

Conclusion

The solution combines Fiori Elements for data entry, CAP for service logic, HANA Cloud for persistence, and SAP Build Process Automation for approval. Success depends on aligning code, runtime state, destinations, credentials, recipients, dependencies, and HDI bindings. Once aligned, users can create, approve or reject, and view Travel requests in one application.

For similar integrations, test each connection independently: Fiori–CAP, CAP–HANA, CAP–BPA, BPA–CAP Actions, and task assignment. This turns a complex landscape into manageable checkpoints.
